maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to stand today and speak on this private member's motion. I must say, as in the case of a good many other motions which have come before this House, this is an example of how effective the idea has been.
The hon. member for Mackenzie is to be heartily congratulated for having brought this matter to the attention of the House. In spite of the fact that the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act pretty well cover the whole sector of grain growing in our nation, and although they have been effective in giving some kind of stability to the grain growing people of Canada, there always has been a deficiency when it comes to those who grow grain which is used on the farm for feeding cattle, poultry or pork.
I was going to say that that has been a serious oversight, but that would be overstating the matter. The fact of the matter is that it is high time that this situation is addressed because in Canada we are so well aware of the need for secondary industry. What the two acts have done is, in a very serious way, hamper the development of secondary industry in agriculture. They put the person who did use the grain on his farm at a disadvantage in so far as other producers in the field were concerned.
This motion goes a long way to alleviating that situation. I understand it has the support of all parties in the House. I think it is a very progressive thing for the Parliament of Canada to be doing.
As I was saying, this motion establishes more firmly the concept of secondary industries within the primary industries in our nation and will go a long way toward doing several things. Hopefully, in so far as the stabilization of the rural economy is concerned, it will help to stop the exodus of people from the rural areas into the cities and should go a long way toward stabilizing the rural populations of our nation in general. The reason for that is it will provide stabilization for the secondary industry and some growth in it as well.
The production of pork, chickens and cattle by the smaller producer will give a stability to these people as well. It will also provide an incentive for people to get away from growing grain only and back into a more labour intensive situation. Again, as I said before, this will help to reduce the depopulation of our rural areas.
There had been some concern expressed in so far as the administration of the program is concerned. I understand that was one of the reasons the concept had not been introduced more rapidly than it has been up to this point. There have been demonstrations in a different context, primarily with the administration in the province of Alberta, in a roundabout way, of getting the Crow benefit to farmers, something which my party and I do not agree with. The idea, the concept, the certainty introduced by the member for Mackenzie that the

April 9, 1990
Private Members' Business
program can be administered is there. It is something which we should all recognize is possible and will work well. Proof of that has been that it is going to be copied, if it has not been already, in the province of Saskatchewan and in the province of Manitoba as well. It may not be too effective to list a great number of the organizations which have supported this idea, but we could certainly include the Canadian Pork Council, the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, the Christian Farmers Federation of Ontario, the Ontario Milk Marketing Board, the Prairie Pools and many other organizations which are almost too numerous to mention.
It is very gratifying that we now have what looks like, almost without question, the support of the House of Commons. Certainly Canadian agriculture will be taking a more stable step forward with the passage of this very important motion introduced by my colleague, the member of Parliament for Mackenzie.

speechtext:
For a minute, Mr. Speaker, I thought I was going to have the hon. member's riding, which is a very rich riding-I probably wouldn't mind it-but mine is rich as well in the great agricultural traditions of Canada. I am delighted to represent my riding. It probably has more pork producers, dairy producers and chicken producers than most other ridings in Canada.
I rise with pleasure to speak on the motion of the hon. member for Mackenzie, as amended by the member for Prince Albert-Churchill River. It doesn't make the changes that have been suggested here this afternoon. It simply proposes that the government consider changes to the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act to allow payment for grains grown on the farm and fed to livestock on that farm.
I support and have supported this principle for many years. Four years ago the mover of this motion and I sat on the agriculture committee when we made a different recommendation which I will read into the record in just a minute.
I support this motion even though I believe it is a little late. It is late because the need was seen five years ago when grain prices first dropped. Payments to the grain farmers were very large at that time and the pork,
chicken, poultry and beef producers were not allowed access to these very large payments.
They saw support going to people who grew their crops on the same type of land right next door to them. They sincerely wanted part of that type of support. But now the five-year average for the crop is so low that the issue is only one of principle. Perhaps in the future if it occurs again in the same set of circumstances, the changes that are suggested here today will have impact and in that light I am delighted to support the motion.
It is too late, as well, I believe, simply because the government has already moved to cover most of the areas concerned. I hope I will have some time later to mention the amount of discussion that has taken place on the safety net proposal. These are discussions that involve many groups and farmers to the point that the agricultural community is almost "discussed out". The farmers hardly have the energy to keep up to the many discussions. The motion comes almost after the fact because we have already moved in this particular area.
I am sure that some of the effects of low grain prices are helped through the stabilization programs that are in place in the red meat sector. But they do not make the wide changes that are built in, which occurred in 1985 and 1986. The farmers like to consider themselves as having two enterprises, the first a grain-growing enterprise and the second a livestock enterprise. I can understand their concern.
Perhaps I could take a moment to add that some of my farmers believe that if they got their subsidy or help in the grain industry, instead of through the red meat industry, then somehow American farmers would not see the stabilization for pork, which has been high in the last little while, as a countervailable item. Somehow they would see it as similar to their deficiency payments and their target prices. Therefore, it is thought, they would not introduce countervail actions.
On the other hand there is also the thought among beef farmers that if we do stabilize grain, then the Americans will indeed see that as a countervailable subsidy which could create the possibility of a countervail action.
I want to go on record as saying that I believe it does not matter how the subsidy arrives in a farmer's hands. If our good, efficient producers can sell a product into the American market and appear to be displacing their producers, then their producers will start a countervail action regardless of the method by which the subsidy is given. Indeed the only solution that is going to stop the countervail program, something which is off the topic
April 9, 1990

here today, is an agreement to net out subsidies which can and will, I hope, be arrived at under the free trade discussion.
About four years ago the mover of this motion, the member for Mackenzie, and I sat on the Standing Committee on Agriculture. At that time we passed a motion which reads: "It should be only for the final products marketed that the producer receives market production under the WGSA or the ASA. In the case of livestock producers, they face the livestock market but not the grain market risk. Treating livestock producers as grain producers means the grain may be covered in the raw form and again as it goes into the final product''.
You will see that while the government did not move to fulfil the area I wanted, it did follow the direction of the Standing Committee on Agriculture and the direction of the member who moved this motion in this session of Parliament. I am very pleased that now, through the safety net proposal, we are moving ahead to consider a different form of support.
What are the problems if we follow this motion? As I said before, it is just a suggestion about future action. One problem will be that we go to production records. We are not talking about sales any more if we are dealing with home-fed grains. We have to figure out how much grain is grown on that particular piece of land, the land base that surrounds almost every livestock operation in Canada. It is a matter of how to get those records. We simply do not have them. We would have to go to regional records. The very good grain producer, the man who produces the big crops through good management, perhaps with better land, would be hurt because he could not get as much stabilization as he should be getting. The poor producer would have a benefit because he would get more than perhaps he should because of his production.
As well, we have the matter of increased costs. We have the costs of getting these records. We have the costs of paying for the stabilization of this home-fed grain. It has been suggested that it is about 20 per cent, which is perhaps high. But it is a significant amount of
Private Members' Business
Canadian grain that is fed on the farm and there would be an increased cost to the government.
There would also be increased costs in the Western Grain Stabilization Act, as it is now established, to the farmer since he pays a premium for this coverage.
In our red meat stabilization program there is a factor built-in. In the case of red meat it is the market price of grain. I believe there is a compensating factor. It is not adequate, but there is some compensation paid in the red meat programs. If we introduce stabilization to home-fed grains, it has always been my belief that somehow we would have to separate these out. I have not been able to work out in my mind how such a separation would occur.
There is another effect concerning the stablization of home-fed grains. In my riding there are many dairy producers. Their cost of production is worked into the price they can charge for their products. So the cost of growing the grain is built into the cost of the very excellent milk, cheese and butter that we buy. Indeed, if the dairy farmers of Ontario, and I am sure those across Canada, were to receive stablization of home-fed grains it would reduce the cost of production and end up reducing the market price of their product. Thus stabilization of home-fed grains is of no advantage to the dairy producers of Canada.
This government has done a lot to help the grain farmers of western Canada. In 1985, we introduced interim stabilization payments in the spring so that they could have help early in the crop year, if a payment were judged to be due in the fall. We have extended the coverage. Nine new crops were brought in in 1988. We made it easier for farmers to rejoin the program. We wrote down a very large deficit in the program to help the grain farmers. This has resulted in a very large increase in participation which was, indeed, the reason why we undertook all of these measures.
Later, in the last five years, we noticed that the stabilization payments were now doing their job to help the farmers simply because we have had a long term of depressed prices. Before 1984, it seemed that we would have one product down while other products were up. Stabilization in the one product would help to smooth

April 9, 1990
out the waters. Now it seems that all product prices are low.
You are indicating, Mr. Speaker, that I have come to the end of my time. I appreciate the opportunity to get a few ideas on the record. I had many more. I am delighted that I and most of my colleagues to whom I have spoken are in favour of this principle, although we feel it is probably too late because the government has already acted to consider it.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure this House will wish to commend the Government of Canada and the government of the Province of Ontario today for their demonstrated dedication to conserving what is one of our planets most precious resources, the soil.
In launching National Soil Conservation Week, the federal and Ontario Ministers of Agriculture announced a $22.2 million agreement to promote the careful management and protection of soil, to prevent its physical and chemical deterioration and to ensure its long term preservation for agriculture and the environment.
April 9, 1990

The cost of the programs under the agreement are shared equally between the two governments. Ottawa's contribution goes to providing more extensive knowledge of soil conservation, technology and practices, and to increasing the awareness by farmers of existing problems and the solutions which are available. Ontario's share goes to the existing Land Stewardship Program, providing grants to encourage rural conservation practices that will improve food production, soil resources and quality of water.
We want to congratulate the two ministers, the Hon. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Agriculture, and the Hon. David Ramsay for the high priority they have committed to conserving our precious soil for future generations.

Last week a Statistics Canada report noted that the poor in Canada are at risk. Put simply, poverty is a health hazard. Nearly one million children in Canada are poor. In Ontario, 200,000 people depend on food banks and half of these are children.

We see the Tory federal government refusing to take the lead and raise the federal minimum wage as a means to redress the most basic need of the working poor-more money.
We see the Ontario Liberal government cut the $1.4 million Emergency Shelter and Assistance Program which helps feed the poor and the homeless. Without it, more will go hungry. It is time governments, both Tory and Liberal, stopped shirking their responsibilities, buried their deceptive rhetoric and took concrete action to assist this country's poor.

In the report, Zero Inflation, the Goal of Price Stability, the C.D. Howe Institute argues that the monetary policy can achieve stable inflation. According to the institute president Thomas Kierans, the goal of price stability is "the only way to go".
In addition, all of the five contributing economists agree that a 5 per cent inflation rate is too high and it should be moved downward to the range of 0 to 2 per cent. Mr. Speaker, like most issues around here, the GST is getting blown out of all proportion. A recent article in a weekly newspaper in my riding stated that the GST would cause senior citizens to lose their homes and not be able to eat. How absolutely absurd.
The GST is simply replacing one tax with another tax very similar to those used by many of the most prosperous countries in the world, countries like West Germany, England, Scotland, Japan, Belgium, Denmark, France and on and on, including Sweden which has some of the most progressive social programs in the world.
I believe that our economy is in urgent need of repair and, unfortunately, the steps required to repair it are not going to be popular. One of these steps is to make sure that our business community will be competitive and one of the ways to do that is to have a competitive tax system similar to those of our competition.
I believe that it is not our God-given right to have one of the highest standards of living in the world, and that we can only have it if we earn it. I also believe that in the years to come it will be even more difficult to earn it because of the growing international competition.
Yes, we will have change and that will be bad enough, but let us keep it in perspective and avoid the hysterics.

The people of Scarborough are especially proud of our long time fire department employee for bringing such honours to Canada. With steady shot making and the support of a talented rink, Ed defeated Scotland 3 to 1 in the final game. This is Ed's second world title and the second consecutive victory for Canada.
Congratulations to Ed Werenich and to his rink, John Kawaja, Ian Tetley and Pat Perroud. You have won a great victory for Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the 1990 budget the minister announced that the crown corporation, Canadian Patents and Development
Ltd. would be wound up and its functions dispersed into 14 government departments.
What the minister ignored was that other departments have said they do not want or need this additional burden. The minister received a submission that showed the cost of such a dispersal would be three times higher than the cost of letting CPDL handle the work.
How can the minister justify this costly action during times of budgetary restraint and so-called deficit reduction? CPDL has played and continues to play an invaluable role in the transfer of technology. It has generated economic benefits and direct revenue to Canada.
The dispersal of CPDL will erode the expertise it now provides and cost the Canadian taxpayers three times as much money for the same service. Obviously government fiscal mismanagement has found another target and the government has shown once again that dogma is more important than common sense.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister.
In Quebec City on Friday, it was reported that the Minister of the Environment said: "We can now imagine a scenario where English Canada will have to choose between Quebec and Newfoundland."
These were discouraging words for Canadians who, I am sure, believe that every federal cabinet minister has an obligation to speak in a way that shows that he or she believes that each and every part of this country is valuable and needed.
Is it the policy' of the government that Canada should ever have to choose between these two provinces? Was the Minister of the Environment speaking for the government when he used the words he used in Quebec City last Friday?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be helpful if the Leader of the Opposition quoted the Minister of the Environment fully. The Minister of the Environment went on to say,


April 9, 1990

and I am quoting him directly: "Nobody thinks Newfoundland should leave Confederation."
That is the position of the Government of Canada and all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has not given a direct answer to my question as to what he has to say about the words that the Minister of the Environment in fact did use.
What constructive result does the Prime Minister think can come out of the special committee that began its work today on the proposals of Premier McKenna, if he allows his senior ministers to go around the country using the kind of language I have quoted as being used by the Minister of the Environment in Quebec City last Friday?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if all the minister said was the quote that my hon. friend chose to use, then obviously my hon. friend would have questions to raise.
However, the Minister of the Environment said: "Nobody thinks Newfoundland should leave Confederation." That is a statement that should satisfy all members of the House, including the Leader of the Opposition.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a third question for the Prime Minister. According to a report today from Canadian Press, an American source involved in the preparations being made for the Canada-U.S. Summit stated that the U.S. President and the Prime Minister of Canada are to discuss the Canadian constitutional deadlock at their meeting this week.
I want to ask the Prime Minister whether this information is correct. If so, wouldn't it be better to discuss this domestic problem with the provincial Premiers and Canadian legislators here in Canada instead of discussing it with a foreign head of State?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend quoted an anonymous American source with reference to a meeting that will take place with the President of the United States. Canada's internal matters will be discussed with Canadians, not with others.
Oral Questions

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last week the Prime Minister told Canadians that he would start a campaign to sell the GST. Why spend millions on advertising if the Prime Minister is so sure that once Canadians have a better understanding of the GST, they will certainly support it? Why not set an example to Canadians by allowing Tory members, who ought to have a good understanding of the GST, a free vote on Bill C-62?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, personally, I believe government members would not be here if they were not capable of listening to Canadians. Canadians also tell us a lot about the GST. Almost every day, several thousand Canadians ask us for explanations, because of the opposition. While you were in power, you brought the finances of this country to the brink. You have always been against everything we did to improve the situation. When we talk to Canadians quietly, as I did only yesterday, when I met people who had been upset by members who may have ulterior motives, other than Canada's economic interests, in fact I talked to them for five minutes, and they told me: We did not know that; thank you very much. I am sure that if we work very hard in the months to come, we will be able to reverse the situation.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister has said that this is a money bill so it becomes a question of confidence in the government for all members to your right, Mr. Speaker, to vote in support of the bill.
I want to ask the Prime Minister specifically whether that means that members of his caucus have by consensus supported the GST, or does it mean that the government is forcing the members of the government to support the GST?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have some grave doubt as to whether that is a question that goes to the administration of the government. I think it is out of order. The hon. member might find a different way to put it.

April 9, 1990
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the question is a very simple question. The Prime Minister himself has said that this is a money bill and that it is a question of confidence in the government.
Is the Prime Minister allowing members of the government to vote according to their conscience or is he forcing a vote? It's a simple question.
Order!
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think I must advise the hon. member that he is trespassing over the line.
The hon. member for Yukon.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the right hon. Prime Minister. Over the weekend and today thousands of Canadians have registered their anger and opposition to the goods and services tax. Today, outside on Parliament Hill we saw yet again working people expressing their opposition to the goods and services tax.
The Prime Minister says that this tax will be good for us. How can he be so right and 80 per cent of Canadians be so wrong? Isn't it time to listen to the voices and votes of Canadians, to stop abusing Parliament and his own back-benchers, and to have a free vote in the House of Commons on the goods and services tax?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the government were choosing to do the easy or popular thing, obviously we would not pursue the goods and services tax.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You wouldn't be at 15 per cent in the polls.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: My hon. friend from the Liberal Party, the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, says that they would not be at 50 per cent in the polls either.
Fifteen per cent is where you are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I remind him that I will let him be at 50 per cent in the polls now, and if we continue to do the right thing for Canada-not what is popular but what is right-we will be in first place on election night.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Prime Minister.
I point out again that Canadians across the country from coast to coast to coast are registering their opposition to the goods and services tax because they know it is an unfair and an unjust tax. They are asking the Prime Minister and the government to listen to their voices.
I say again to the Prime Minister: Will he not listen to the voices of Canadians; will he not listen to the constituents of his members as well and have a free vote in the House of Commons?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend asks whether we have listened to the voices of Canadians. Yes, indeed, we have. We have listened and read very carefully the reports of five Royal commissions and task forces of the Government of Canada over some 40 years, recommending that the Parliament of Canada summon the courage to rid the nation of a pernicious and very unfair manufacturers' sales tax which kills jobs in Canada and imposes an undue penalty on Canadian producers.
We have listened and analyzed very carefully the objective data of five Royal commissions and important studies and we say in the interest of Canada get rid of this pernicious and unfair 13.5 per cent manufacturers' sales tax and substitute a 7 per cent goods and services tax.
We have listened. We are doing that, not because it is popular, and it is clearly not popular, but we are doing so because it is right for Canada. It must be done.
Hear, hear!

My supplementary question is for the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker.
Clearly the Prime Minister is saying that there will not be a voice for democracy in this House and a free vote on the goods and services tax.

The Prime Minister claims the GST is advanced. I find that surprising. The Prime Minister knows perfectly well that charitable organizations, for instance, work for the
April 9, 1990

public good and that they are indispensable. How can he say a tax is advanced if it taxes charitable organizations?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party referred to a tax as not being very advanced and not very sensitive to social concerns. I may remind her that two socialist governments introduced that kind of tax in their own countries, so it can't be that bad.
We have had long and thorough consultations with charitable organizations, and would urge the Leader of the New Democratic Party to read the technical papers which explain that we have set in place a series of mechanisms so that these organizations will not be penalized far from it by this tax reform.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
From what we have heard so far of the minister's aid package for the troubled Atlantic fishery, the government has decided to focus on getting people out of the fishery.
We see no specific evidence of any increased commitment to scientific evaluation and no new efforts to develop the under-utilized species and thereby remove the foreigners from our 200-mile zone.
Does the minister not think it would be wiser to be sure about the stocks and to be sure that we have fully developed all available species before we tell the people that they must give up their life's work and the traditions of all those communities dependent on the fishery?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I agree.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the minister is going to put the emphasis on scientific evaluation and on the under-utilized species. I hope that when we do see the supposed package we will see that; that it will be seen that there needs to be a new mesh size for all sectors in the fishery, that there will be new scientific evaluations in the waters around Nova Scotia.
Oral Questions
But for the 2,000 people who met in Digby under very extreme conditions on Saturday, it is not a solution to hear the minister say: "Yes, we agree". We want to see what you are going to do. We do not need money. We want to see that you are going to give a commitment to keep the jobs in the fishery.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to hear, for the first time in several months, a Liberal member of Parliament asking the government not to throw money at the problem. I thank her for her recommendation.
What the government will do with the situation in the fishery in Atlantic Canada is to devise methods whereby we can assert the federal role in the fisheries and work in co-operation with the fishermen and the provinces to ensure that we can have a viable fishery, ensuring a good income for fishermen and plant workers.
We also want to continue what this government has been working on since 1984, that is, trying to diversify the economy of Atlantic Canada so that our kids in Atlantic Canada can have a bright future there. That is what we are working on.
I can advise the member that my meetings with fishermen, union representatives in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, and the leaders of these provinces led me to conclude that we are on the right course. I will continue to listen to them so that I can have their input and develop something that may not be nice for grandstanding on the issue but that will be relevant to the needs of those people.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Supply and Services, I will directed my question to the Prime Minister.
This weekend we learned of allegations that the request for proposals for the $28.5 million east coast air surveillance contract was deliberately written to exclude all other bidders except Atlantic Airways, a company that just happens to be represented by one of the Prime Minister's close pals, John Lundrigan.

April 9, 1990
Oral Questions
How can the Prime Minister justify this apparent sole sourcing of a $30 million contract which brings into serious question the integrity of the entire public tendering process?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I happened to be in Atlantic Canada, in St. John's, with my colleague, the Minister for International Trade, where we advised people in Atlantic Canada of what the Department of Fisheries and Oceans would be doing in terms of surveillance.
The Liberal Party may well be interested in trying to find mud in all of this, but the people down there know that twice as much surveillance will take place in Atlantic Canada by those aircraft. That is what the people were very, very happy with.
That this company in St. John's, Newfoundland had the new technologies to ensure that it could become a leader, not only in Canada but world-wide, should be applauded by the hon. member instead of trying to throw mud at it.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party is not against additional surveillance, but the Liberal Party is certainly against the awarding of contracts based not on the merit of the proposal but on the political connection of the lobbyist.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was very patient for the first question, but I am afraid we will have to move on.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment.
Most Canadians are aware that the environmental record of this federal government is extremely poor, particularly on issues like the Oldman River dam and the Rafferty-Alameda.
Since the Minister of the Environment is fully aware that Quebec Hydro is proceeding with James Bay II, or the Great Whale Project as it is known, without federal approvals, why is the minister continuing to duck his responsibilities to put a panel in place which has a credible time frame to evaluate the impact upon the Inuit and the Cree, fish, migratory birds, caribou, whales, methane, and global warming, all those impacts that are clearly in federal jurisdiction, or will the studies be done
after the dams are built as we saw in Saskatchewan and Alberta?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the member would at least read the newspapers, he would know that as a government we are dedicated to the environment, that we have rejected-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question was put and the other side listened to the question. The minister is rising to answer it, and I would ask all hon. members to allow the minister to speak.

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
We announced last Friday that this government is rejecting the plan proposed by Quebec on the kind of joint assessment that Quebec would like to do. We said that Quebec's proposal does not respect the standards of efficiency and rigour that the federal government would like to have in this assessment.
We stated that we would present a counterproposal, probably this week, where we will state all of our requirements and try to reach a joint assessment with Quebec. If we are unable to reach an agreement on this, the federal government will proceed alone on a separate environmental assessment.

Mr. Speaker, as the minister is aware, Quebec Hydro is busy selling the power from James Bay II, is busy building the roads and is busy clearing the land for the dam construction project for those five river valleys.
Could the minister be somewhat more specific in terms of time frame, in terms of information access and in terms of when exactly a federal panel will be composed? Canadians, and particularly Canadians in the province of Quebec, want to know when the panel is going to start its work. Is it going to be now when the terms of the project can be carefully defined and the information necessary to define such a project can be done before the project is well under way?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal government has very clear jurisdiction in the area of environmental impact assessment. This jurisdiction is not challenged-it cannot be challenged-particularly in the case of James Bay. However, we must admit that Quebec's position poses a problem, because Quebec would give the commission only about four months to do the environmental assessment. The federal government believes that the commission must be given the time it needs to do a proper assessment that will assure the people of Quebec and of
April 9, 1990

Canada that the James Bay project will have no negative impact. No one is in a position to lecture us on this subject. We are pursuing a national policy so that the requirements of the federal process are respected throughout the country-in the West, in central Canada, in Quebec and in the Maritimes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Second Storey Women's Centre in Bridgewater has delayed its acceptance of project funding for two reasons: first, because those women do not want to be in competition for small amounts of money with all the other women's centres in the country and, second, because they still have a hope that this government might reinstate the $1.6 million in core funding.
Will the Secretary of State melt his and his colleagues' stony hearts, spend this small amount of money, and save all the women's centres in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I was very clear when I said that core funding was discontinued for the women's centres.
I did indicate that there was increased project funding that was available. I have opened up the criteria so that certain admissible expenses, which were formerly only admitted under core funding, would now be considered under the project application.
I am waiting anxiously to make sure that any application that is received will receive expeditious treatment so that the money can flow. We are anxious to make sure that whatever funding we have available is made available to those who can carry on the very excellent work that they have had to do in the past.

Mr. Speaker, one of the reasons that the women at Second Storey have some hope that the government might change its mind is that they met on Friday with the minister's colleague, the
Oral Questions
Minister responsible for the Status of Women. In Halifax she promised that she would lobby her cabinet colleagues, and in particular the Secretary of State, to meet with representatives of all of the women's centres affected so that they could be certain that they were not in competition with each other for every small amount of money in project funding and so that they could possibly convince the minister how crucial core funding is.
Although the Minister responsible for the Status of Women is not here, can the Secretary of State say today to the women of Canada that he will meet with the representatives from all these centres together and give them some hope?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will be meeting with representatives of women's centres tomorrow.
Together?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext: I will be meeting again on Thursday with representatives of women's centres.
But not together.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext: As far as I am concerned, I am willing to talk. I would like to continue a dialogue. I would like to make sure that our program, which is available, is there to be effective in helping the women's centres to carry on with their work.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.
On February 14, the Minister of National Health and Welfare was asked to address the current economic crisis in which 1.4 million Canadians, including over one-half a million children, are forced to rely on food banks.
Today, as the Daily Bread Food Bank kicks off its Easter food drive, this government is still doing nothing to help the poor, the homeless, and the hungry.

April 9, 1990
Oral Questions
What is this government doing to end the reliance on food banks? Why will it not take full responsibility for helping to feed the victims of its own economic mismanagement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a very specific question with a very global approach. We are aware that all such prevailing situations are related to social, sociological, economic and political conditions. Our programs are designed to help all classes in society, of course including children, families and women. We are concerned about such issues as health, welfare and our participation as a government. The answer lies in the interest we show in all these programs.

Mr. Speaker, the only growth that this government has had is in the line ups at the food banks. The dependence on food banks has doubled in 1988.
Studies show that between the federal CAP cut-backs, the cruel changes to the UI eligibility formula, and the GST thousands of more Canadians will be forced into poverty. How can the minister justify her answer when she knows that this government's policies will directly increase the number of poor Canadians?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to respond to my hon. friend who raises a very sensitive and important matter. Since the general question involves poverty, she will be the first to applaud the fact that since the swearing in of this government almost 800,000 Canadians have been removed from the poverty rolls in Canada.
In fact, since 1984 the number of children living below the poverty level has fallen by 259,000, compared to an increase of 283,000 between 1980 and 1984 when her party was in office.
Also, it is probably significant for my hon. friend to note that on Friday morning when Statistics Canada reported unemployment figures, the unemployment rate in Canada has now dropped to the lowest since August 1981. Since this government was sworn in, 1,587,000
more Canadians are working today than when we took over from the Liberals.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister will be aware at this point in time that there is overwhelming opposition to the GST throughout Canada due to the fact that Canadians perceive that the system is inherently unfair. They point to the fact that there were 93,000 profitable corporations that did not pay any tax in 1987.
Does the Prime Minister not recognize the blatant unfairness of this fact, that these corporations pay no corporate tax at all. Will he at least commit himself and his government to bringing in a minimum corporate tax?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member and many colleagues in his party keep repeating this information which is wrong. There is no such thing as 93,000 profit making corporations that do not pay tax and we on this side of the House have changed that.
Due to measures taken during the crisis, a lot of loopholes were built into our fiscal system. We have removed them one by one, and now all large corporations pay taxes.
What he refers to are very often small farms and small businesses that have not been profitable for five years and frequently earn less than $25,000. Would the hon. gentleman want us to tax them and put them out of business? Frequently they are not taxed because they are in remote areas where there is a high level of unemployment. This is a good measure and, like the GST, it is a fair tax.
Yet again there is opposition because the member, instead of accepting his responsibility to help Canadians extricate themselves from a difficult financial situation, does everything he can to mislead the population.
I have a supplementary, Mr. Speaker, again to the Prime Minister. The minister who has just answered has suggested that we are not giving the figures correctly.

Exactly!
April 9, 1990

Oral Questions

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member will put his question.

The figures that I have provided to the House are the figures from Statistics Canada as we requested them. It was a study that Statistics Canada did for the New Democratic Party in 1987.
The minister said that was before tax reform. In 1988, these were some of the small corporations: Xerox Canada, $74 million, no tax at all; Bramalea Corporation, $33 million, no tax at all; Brascan Corporation, there is a small one, $263 million and not a penny of tax. That is 1988, after tax reform.
In view of the fact that tax reform in 1988 has just created another tax holiday for all of these large corporations, not small corporations, not family businesses, large wealthy corporations, is the minister prepared now to make them pay their fair share-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. minister.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
The
great trouble, Mr. Speaker, with the hon. gentleman is that he loves listening to himself. He should listen to me and to us as well.
Perhaps he was away, but I would like to welcome him to the 1990s. He is giving figures from 1987. He does not seem to be aware that we have a tax on assets. Any corporation, not with profits, but with assets of $10 million pays tax. We are collecting billions of dollars from them, but he fails to mention that. He claims again the old repetitions. Canadians understand that these reforms are there to help the economy of Canada and to create jobs. This is what we have been doing and will continue to do.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It is hardly necessary for me to describe the panic and anxiety felt by many Canadians of Lebanese origin. Is the minister aware of charges made against the Immigration and Refugee Board that it is insensitive and indifferent with respect to people applying for refugee status here in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, the refugee board operates at arm's length from the government. Whereas we established the board, this is a judicial process set up under an arm's length arrangement with that board.
My understanding is that the board is functioning quite well. If there are problems, and if he has a particular allegation to bring to me, I would be happy to ensure that it gets looked into.

Mr. Speaker, I can assure the minister that I will be filing complaints with her office in a few days.
My question is directed to the Prime Minister. Do you not feel that time has come for the government to intervene in the case of refugees of Lebanese origin who are experiencing great hardships? They need understanding and compassion in such trying times.
Good question!

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our government is highly sensitive to the situation of Lebanese people. Because of the on-going war, refugees go to Cyprus or Damascus and apply to come to Canada-
We have set extra people in Cyprus in order to be able to deal sympathetically and effectively with the Lebanese. We are working very hard on their behalf, and we will continue to do so.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 80 per cent of Canadians are saying no to the government. The people are mad, angry and disappointed with the goods and services tax. Never in the history of Canada have so many people said no so many times to a government bill.
There are only two reasonable choices left for this government: either scrap the tax, or call an election. Which one will the government choose?

April 9, 1990
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would call an election, but I cannot out of fairness. They do not have a leader.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: We beat you the last time, remember?
That's what Joe said in 1979.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
I just want to draw to the hon. member's attention comments made by Mr. Chretien with regard to the manufacturers' sales tax and the commodity tax system. He stated: "It worries me that serious structural problems have been identified in the manufacturers' sales tax. To name just a few, in some cases its burden falls less heavily upon imported goods than upon domestic goods. It falls unevenly upon competing goods which are marketed at different trade levels. It does not currently permit a meaningful appeals system. These problem areas in the law cannot be tolerated indefinitely."
Then Mr. Chretien said: "Before long, I will have to assess the merits of all opinions and make a decision on the best course to follow." That was on November 22, 1977.

Mr. Speaker, we are ready for an election when the government is ready for it.
We always acknowledged a need for reform in the tax system, but we never called on someone to hit the people on the head with a two by four. That is exactly what this particular tax does.

How can the government continue to ignore the workers, small businesses, seniors and low- and middle-income Canadians who have done all they could to get the government to listen to them? When will the government finally listen to Canadians and withdraw this unfair tax?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, given the demand that my friend makes, one would think that there would be a consistent approach from his political party.
Yet on March 7 in The Globe and Mail Mr. Martin is quoted as saying:
- that he would scrap the 7 per cent tax if he becomes Prime Minister and "if it is humanly possible," but he refused to rule out some sort of consumption tax as an alternative.
On Monday, Douglas Young, the Liberals' finance critic, also said the party would scrap the GST if it came into power, but he was unclear on an alternative.
Thirteen years later, after making the first speech, Mr. Chretien said it would be irresponsible for the Liberals to decide now on scrapping the GST. "We cannot reasonably make a commitment that there will not be a consumption tax".

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
A year and a half after the slaughter of 3,000 pro-democracy demonstrators in Burma, the military government has forcibly relocated hundreds of thousands of its citizens and imprisoned, tortured and even murdered many opposition leaders in preparation for phoney elections.
Petro-Canada, which has signed a $5 million contract with that government, says that none of this is of its concern. Is this the future of a privatized Petro-Canada? Will it prop up oppressive regimes, even those condemned by our government? Or will the government take action to end this arrangement, and do it now?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:

You hope.

Let us have a look at what Dr. Maslove, an economics professor here in Ottawa, had to say regarding the government's so-called tax reform since it took office. The effect of lower rates and other actions during the phase one of tax reform has been examined by Dr. Maslove of Carleton University. Using a Statistics Canada model to assess the effects of changes in the personal income tax system since 1984, Dr. Maslove has determined that the only real beneficiaries of tax reform are those whose annual incomes are under $10,000 or over $114,490. The federal government is losing over $30 billion annually as a result of tax shelters, special grants and incentives to business. It has been observed in this regard that, if the corporate sector's tax share had matched that of individual taxpayers in 1988, Canada would have enjoyed an $18.5 billion surplus instead of a $30 billion deficit.
What we see is a continuation of what the Liberals did when they were in office, only in a much more blatant form under the Conservatives. The Liberals always liked to funnel all of the special tax shelters and grants to certain corporations and to certain very wealthy people, but the Tories have really taken it to heart and are now directing the majority of tax breaks to the extremely wealthy and to those corporations which funnel lots of cash back to the government at election time.

The wholesaler pays $113.50, tax included. Assuming the wholesaler has a profit margin of 10 per cent, he sells the chair to the furniture store for $124.85. No tax is collected on this transaction. If the retailer takes a 10 per cent profit, he sells you the chair for $137.35. The federal tax does not appear on your bill, but you are paying it just the same because it is included in the selling price. That is the present system.
This tax raises $18 billion annually for Ottawa. Mr. Wilson's proposal consists in abolishing this tax and replacing it with the GST". This means getting rid of the present 13.5 per cent tax and replacing it with a tax on goods and services that will be 7 per cent across the board. In the end, the consumer will pay only 7 per cent on what he purchases and not the present 13.5 per cent manufacturer's tax.
He repeated the same example with the new tax, and I quote: "The new 7 per cent tax will apply at all stages of production and distribution. Consider our example. The manufacturer sells the chair to the wholesaler for $100. The wholesaler pays $7 in tax. He does not add the $7 to his cost, since Ottawa will refund the tax when he sells the chair. The wholesaler adds his 10 per cent profit, sells the chair to the furniture dealer for $110 and claims his $7 refund from Ottawa. The dealer will pay $7.70 in GST. After adding his profit margin, he sells you the chair for $121 and claims a refund of $7.70 from the government. You, the consumer will pay 7 per cent tax,

"The GST is regressive in the sense that it is harder on low income people. Both the man on social welfare and the millionnaire will pay the $7 tax on a $100 chair. Had Mr. Wilson not done anything to correct that the TPS would be unfair and scandalous.
But the minister did provide for compensation to offset the GST impact on poor households through tax credits geared to income, family status and number of children. These credits will be paid by cheques on a quarterly basis."
Then he gives examples. This is important, Mr. Speaker, because it is the basic argument in the GST issue. It says here, and I agree: It would be a regressive tax if there were no tax credits. But, as it happens, there are major tax credits. He gives one example: "A retired widow with a $12,000 income will get a $290 tax credit. She would have to spend at least $4,000 on goods and services (other than rent and food)-", and drugs. She would have to spend $4,000 a year to cancel the value of her tax credit, or not to end up a loser "-to cancel the value of that credit. That is highly unlikely."
Again, Mr. Speaker, I quote the article. "A single-parent family made up of a child and a young woman earning a net income of $16,000 will get a $480 credit, or almost $10 a week. To annul the credit the household would have to spend something like $140 a week on taxable goods and services." Again, on goods and services, other than rent, food and drugs. A single parent family earning $16,000 a year would therefore have to spend a $140 a week, on something other than non-taxable basic items to, cancel the value of the credit received.
The article continues: "Finally, a couple with two children with a combined net income of $25,000 will receive a credit of $580.

I continue: "As a matter of fact, if your family income is less than $30,000, you are among the winners. If it is more, you are among the loosers, because you will not be entitled to the tax credit, although you will have to pay the GST just the same."
Because I now realize that my time is coming to an end, Mr. Speaker, I wish to conclude by saying that the GST is good for the Canadian economy and good for Canadian exporters and importers. It is also good for Canadians whose income is less than $30,000 and who, as I said, will come out winners with this new tax to replace the 66 year old 13.5 per cent federal sales tax.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let's not kid ourselves about what is happening here. The GST is a tax on consumption. It means that every time you buy anything, you, the individual Canadian consumer, are going to pay more.

Because it is regressive, it will hurt most low and middle income families who can the least afford to pay it. It is a tax which goes against all the promises which this Government has made in terms of tax fairness and which forces all low and midde income Canadians to shoulder the most unfair tax burden in our history.

It is nothing more than the Canadian version of Margaret Thatcher's new poll tax. Why are they rioting in Britain? Why are they saying: "Axe the poll tax"? It is because it is an unfair tax.
I am not suggesting violence as we have seen in the United Kingdom, but Canadians have a right to be outraged. Canadians are upset about the GST for the same reasons Britons are upset about the poll tax-it is an unfair tax.
April 9, 1990



Mr. Speaker, over 80 per cent of Canadians are against this tax. Canadians, by the hundreds of thousands, have signed petitions, sent letters and protested against this tax, just as they did again today on the Hill.

Canadians realize it is going to be a massive change, not only in the way we are taxed but on what we pay federal taxes.
As my colleague from Ottawa South has pointed out, corporations as such will no longer pay a federal sales tax, but people will. It is the biggest corporate tax grab in history, and nobody but the Minister of Finance thinks companies will pass all their savings from this on to consumers before applying the new goods and services tax.
The GST is a tax on just about everything-all goods, all services, with very limited exceptions. Let us look at a typical day under the new tax regime.
Picture this. You wake up, shut off your new alarm clock, a clock for which you paid 7 per cent more. You brush your teeth with toothpaste and a brush for which you paid 7 per cent more. You use soap, 7 per cent more; towel, 7 per cent more; dress children for school, 7 per cent more for shirts, shoes, socks, dresses; hand them their school books, 7 per cent more for the books; get into the car, 7 per cent more for the car; flat tire on the way to work, 7 per cent more for repairs; park the car, 7 per cent more for parking; at work, have a coffee break, 7 per cent more; have lunch, pick up a sandwich, 7 per cent more, bowl of soup, 7 per cent more, cup of tea, 7 per cent more, dessert, 7 per cent more; drive home, stop for gas, 7 per cent more; stop at the hardware store for a can of paint for the children's room, 7 per cent more; a paint brush, 7 per cent more; stop for a haircut, 7 per cent more; pick up a hockey stick, a baseball bat or a doll for one of the kids, 7 per cent more; pick up a pizza or other take-out food for a quick dinner for you and your family, 7 per cent more; after dinner, sit down to write your cheques for utility bills, the gas bill, 7 per cent more, the electricity bill, 7 per cent more, send the cheque to the lawyer who did the legal work for the purchase of your new house, 7 per cent more for the fees, and that is in

addition to the 7 per cent more you paid for the house and you are still waiting for the rebate cheque from the government for half of it. Call a plumber to fix the leak in the bathroom sink, 7 per cent more; sit in your new chair that cost you 7 per cent more; walk across your new rug, 7 per cent more; read a book, 7 per cent more; have a midnight snack, 7 per cent more.
And if all of this is too much for a taxpayer who drops dead, that will cost the taxpayer 7 per cent more, as well, because this tax even applies to funerals-even they are 7 per cent more.
The only way Canadians can avoid paying the tax is to stop eating anything which is not defined as basic groceries by the bureaucrats at the Department of Finance, and that is not very much; do not buy any more clothes or shoes; unplug the phone; unplug the TV; unplug the fridge; turn off all the lights; shut off the electricity; turn off the furnace; sit in the basement; and, above all, do not die.
Every time a Canadian pays this goods and services tax he or she is going to be thinking about how this tax came to be and who imposed it.

Canadians will remember the dishonest way the government tried to bring in this tax. We had a government in 1979 and a finance minister, Mr. Crosbie, that were prepared to come to grips with certain realities in this country. One of them was simply that if we as Canadians want services and programs from government, we must be willing to pay for them.
In 1979, Mr. Crosbie rose in this House and presented his budget, a budget that would have raised gas 18 cents a gallon, bringing the price up to $1.17 a gallon. That was a budget that the then finance minister claimed to be a budget of short-term pain for long-term gain, but members of the opposition of this House chose to defeat it. In defeating it they defeated the best opportunity that this country has had since Confederation to come to grips with reality.
Now opposition members want to do the same thing with the goods and services tax. But there is one element that these characters are missing this time. They are missing the number of votes required to defeat it, thank goodness.
When we took office in 1984, after having lived through those Trudeau years from 1979 to 1984, we inherited a $200 billion debt. I challenge anyone on the opposition side of this House to dispute that figure. It is there; it is recorded. You can look at it yourselves. It is undeniable.
We have been in power almost six years. On that $200 billion debt, with an 11 per cent interest rate, on average, we have paid interest charges of $132 billion on the debt that the Liberals gave us.

When they left office they bragged. Some of the former cabinet ministers in that Trudeau government bragged that when Brian Mulroney took office there was no way, no way possible that that guy or his party could get re-elected. They said: "We left the cupboard bare. There is no money. There is no room for you people to manoeuvre".
But we have manoeuvred. We have done the things that are right for this country, and we are going to continue to do the things that are right for this country.
I have something to tell the Leader of the Opposition. The members on our side of the House are going to support this tax bill, and we are going to support it for a very good reason. I do not want to mortgage my children or my grandchildren to pay off the debt that we have incurred in this country. We can come to grips with it today or we can come to grips with it tomorrow. But I prefer to face reality square in the face because that is what the people back home put me here for.
In 1986, our government tabled a White Paper on tax reform in this House of Commons. That White Paper, laid before the Canadian people was the goods and services tax, among other things.
In the 1988 election every member of this House, every candidate that ran in that election knew what was coming. The goods and services tax was clearly on the table. It was an issue and part of our platform in 1988.
I ran on that issue, as I did on other issues, and so did the member for Calgary Northeast, as well as the member for Edmonton Southeast, the Kindy and Kil-gour act. Those characters knew the goods and services tax were coming. They knew it very clearly.
Do you know what that same member for Edmonton Southeast did in 1986 and 1987, Mr. Speaker? He sneaked out of the Conservative caucus because we were not high in the polls. Do you know what he is doing now, Mr. Speaker? He is doing the same thing. He came crawling back in 1988 when Brian Mulroney brought this party back up in the polls. He made sure he was on board-

The present tax is a silent killer of jobs. It discriminates against home grown products, home manufactured products. I could draw many examples right in my riding where we are discriminated against because of the present federal sales tax.

Agreed.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte does not realize how often his speech today will be quoted by his Liberal opponent in the next election.
The fact of the matter is that Canadians are very upset. They oppose the thought of another tax. They have seen, since 1984, an increase in the federal sales tax. They have seen this tax go up from 9 per cent to 10 per cent, and then from 11 per cent to 12 per cent, and from 13 per cent to 13.5 per cent-an increase of 50 per cent.
Canadians know that this type of tax is unfair. They know that it applies the same whether you are rich or poor. In other words, it is a regressive kind of tax.
This is, of course, an ideological point that escapes the mind of the average Conservative politician who insists on using a sales tax as an instrument for raising funds, no matter how it applies.
Canadians, I would submit, want fairness in the tax system. They would like now, at last, to see a tax system that also introduces a degree of discipline in our behaviour in the environment. The sales tax as proposed by this government ignores the environment completely. Actually, it does a disservice to the environment.
On the one hand, it reduces the tax on cars, as has been announced, obviously by virtue of the nature of the general sales tax. But, on the other hand-and now I am quoting two extremes-it should not tax any equipment, any service or any type of initiative that is energy efficient, that is efficient in the use of water and of our natural resources. It applies the same sledge-hammer on everything, without any consideration for the environ-
April 9, 1990

ment to which this government has committed itself on a variety of occasions and, extensively so, by way of the notion of sustainable development.
The government may want to know, rather than being criticized, what the alternatives are that it should have considered, and which it can still consider.
There is a substantial body of work that has been carried out in developing some kind of a carbon tax, a taxation of fuels, a taxation that would be dependent on the amount of carbon dioxide that is released when consumed. It has been developed quite extensively by an organization whose name is the Quebec Union for Conservation of Nature in Charlesbourg.
This tax would be calculated on the basis of $130 per tonne of oil equivalent. Such a tax could generate up to $17.2 billion in revenue. It would even reduce the number of officials in charge of collecting it. This tax would encourage, as a result, fuel efficiency in all industrial applications. It would improve our economic competitiveness. It would lead to higher productivity and a better ability on our side to be effective on world markets.
If that taxation measure is not adequate or interesting enough, the Minister of Finance-and I am glad to see his junior colleague in the House today-could have a good conversation with Professor Rees at the University of British Columbia. Here we see the development of an entropy taxation. Professor Rees argues that instead of subsidies to hydrocarbons, Canada should place a tax on fossil fuels on the economically sound ground that atmospheric capacity to absorb carbon dioxide is a scarce resource for which the consumer should pay.
Of course, this type of tax should vary for different fossil fuels, depending on the carbon content per unit of energy. It would be twice as much for coal as for natural gas. Such a tax would then have the effect of lowering the consumption of hydrocarbons, encourage conservation, reduce carbon dioxide pollution and increase considerably our over all energy efficiency.
If the minister is not satisfied with home grown suggestions for an eco-tax reform, we invite him to look across the Atlantic to Europe, with which he is very familiar as we all know, at the University of Cologne in
Government Orders
the Federal Republic of Germany. Policies have been developed there for a green tax reform which include a carbon tax proposal, taxes on throwaway packaging, taxes on junk mail, and taxes on water consumption. The estimate is that a package of green taxes would produce revenues over the long term of well over $100 billion at the current rate of exchange. I am sure, if the Minister of Finance had a chance to read these papers, he would be tempted to withdraw his GST proposal and go the eco-tax route.
One has inevitably in this debate to raise the question of The Green Plan because it is relevant in its economic instruments chapter to this debate. We find an absence of ideas as to what could be the economic instruments and the taxation instruments for this government if it wants to pursue economic goals.
Unlike other sections of the Green Paper where questions are asked, there is no question asked in the economic investment and instruments section. However, it does ask some earth-shaking questions such as: Should the government emphasize compliance or enforcement in general terms? The paper does ask how regulatory procedures can be clarified and streamlined in general terms.
When we come to economic instruments, I must say to the Minister of State for Finance that his colleague, the Minister of the Environment, needs help very badly and very urgently because this process that has been launched by virtue of this discussion on the environment is so weak on the economic side that it makes you weep in despair.
What can we say at this stage of the debate? We can only repeat that Canadians have seen over the last six years a 50 per cent increase in the federal sales tax. They know that it is an unfair instrument. They know that there are alternatives which would be desirable both in terms of fairness and in terms of progress to be made in the environment.
Therefore we have to conclude that this entire exercise is anachronistic. The government has missed the boat with this kind of approach. Not only that, but it has done itself irreparable harm politically as reflected in the polls every month.

Mr. Speaker, today, as on many recent days, members of this House have the opportunity to debate the GST bill and, through

April 9, 1990
Government Orders
that debate, bring improvements to this important legislation.
Unfortunately today, as on many recent days, members of the opposition are wasting their time and the time of this House on a carnival side-show designed to demonstrate to Canadians that they are against the GST.
This spectacle of delay and obstruction is telling us other things as well. It is telling all Canadians that the NDP and Liberal Party have again found the basis for a partnership in futility and waste. It is telling Canadians that some members of Parliament will sacrifice not just time, money and their personal dignity in search of a few seconds of TV news, they are also willing to sacrifice the parliamentary process itself.
There are clear rules designed to allow members of Parliament to do our work. Along with our obligations as members of Parliament we receive certain privileges and entitlements. Among those privileges is the ability to slow down the process when there is reason to believe that a government is exceeding its authority or acting in haste. However, the opposition is making a tragic mistake if it believes that Canadians want them to damage or destroy the parliamentary system itself.
Over time the parliamentary system of government has evolved to become the instrument through which the people of this country govern this country; nothing more, nothing less. This is where things get done. The government has a responsibility to govern, but what are the responsibilities of the opposition? Short of forming a government themselves, how do they measure achievement? How do they justify their existence? What are their responsibilities?
Over the past few weeks we have seen a curious fate overtake members of the opposition who have carried their opposition to the GST bill beyond the limits of reason, if not the limits of parliamentary procedure.
Their systematic refusal to deal with the GST bill on its merits has serious consequences for the people they were elected to represent and for the process of parliamentary government itself. Their obstruction may have started life as a sincere attempt to show their opposition, but as the days and weeks rolled by it became more and more clear that they were not refusing to speak out
because of their opposition to the GST but because, quite literally, they had nothing to say.
Time and again we have challenged members of the opposition to present us with clear alternatives to a national tax on goods and services. Time and again they have failed to respond.
The concept of a Canadian goods and services tax has been discussed for several years. In more recent months the GST has passed through various stages by which the ideas mature and develop to become legislation and the law of the land.
It is interesting to note that as Bill C-62 has assumed a more definitive shape in reality the members who oppose this legislation have become less interested in the details of its operation. As various groups-and we have heard hundreds-have focused on its implementation and its impacts, members of the opposition have devoted more of their attention to obstructing the process by which work gets done in this House and in its committees.
The fate which has overtaken these opposition members is irrelevancy. In a very real sense they have taken it upon themselves to serve as road-blocks and obstacles at a time when their constituents need their intelligence and reasoning abilities the most.
By now it should seem clear to even the most sincere opponents of GST that this government has committed itself to a course of action which it believes is right. So far we have not heard arguments that would turn us from this course.
By now it should be clear that this government knows how to listen to groups and individuals who come forward with sound and reasonable advice. Much of this advice is now incorporated in this bill. The finance committee, of which I am member, travelled across this country and heard from groups and individuals from every province and territory in Canada. Over 300 individuals and groups of witnesses read over 1,000 representations to the finance committee on the GST. This all-party finance committee recommended 70 amendments to this bill after listening to Canadians across the country who want to deal constructively with the GST.
The opposition in refusing to deal with this legislation on its merits exclude itself from improving it. By stubborn, blind, across the board antagonism, the opposition
April 9, 1990

is turning its back on reality and is turning its back on the people it represents.
The people do not elect members of Parliament to create confusion. They do not vote for ignorance. They do not vote for delays, obstruction and waste. They vote for leadership. If the opposition wants to give us the monopoly on leadership, then we have no choice but to accept.
One of the few pleasures of opposition is the ability to ignore reality. There is nothing quite as intoxicating as the ability to build a better future by breaking every rule of arithmetic, logic and common sense.
However the great concern of government is economic reality. Look at free trade. Look at the privatization of Crown corporations. Look at the improved management of government spending. These are all controversial issues. They attracted a great deal of opposition but they all got done.
Let us suppose for a moment that this government took the same all for nothing attitude that the opposition demonstrates. Under those circumstances it is quite possible that the measures I have just mentioned and the GST itself would be vastly different from what they are today. This government does listen to Canadians; we listen to all Canadians. When it comes time to take action we act and we act decisively.
Bill C-62 the GST bill is no different. It has changed over time as this government received the benefit of advice from every region and every sector of this country. This legislation is better because Canadians responded on its merits. They did not dream of a world where corporations can somehow pay taxes without raising prices to consumers. They did not dream of a world where personal income taxes can be increased year after year with no impact on the economy. They responded with realistic and practical solutions to the challenge we place before them.
We on the finance committee, all parliamentarians, should be grateful for the people who took the time to appear before the finance committee, people from all across Canada with constructive advice to criticize the bill in some cases but to improve it, to discuss it on its merits, not just to be wasteful and obstructionist like the opposition MPs in the House.

Here we are again today. This is the debate on report stage. Time is running short and soon time will run out. This government knows what it is doing. We have a list of objectives. We are here. We want to get the deficit under control. That is why we have acted to bring government expenditures under control and have introduced the GST bill, Bill C-62.
We want to build an economy that can fight and win against international competition. That is why we negotiated the free trade agreement and introduced Bill C-62. We want a fair tax system. That is why we reformed the corporate and personal income tax system, and that is why we introduced Bill C-62. A great deal of work remains to be done. There is still time for opposition members to abandoned their ill-conceived and foolish struggle and get down to some real work.
