We have a clear example here, through the member from Sault Ste. Marie, of all the problems that these members are creating by choosing to use a major tax reform politically instead of looking at the good of the country.
Instead of saying what he has just told this House, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie should open up the book we have produced to explain the technical papers. He should read and he will have answers for his constituents. His duty is not only to report, it is also to enlighten and explain calmly to his constituents that the problem is not at all what they hear.
The list is long. He talked about music lessons and so on. He knows full well that the impact will not be the one that is feared and he should assist the government in
Government Orders
this reform by explaining to citizens of his riding how this reform will work. They may not like it afterward, but they should at least try to have the correct information. We on our side at least, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, will continue to work very hard over the coming months to explain to Canadians the importance of this reform.
As an example of information that is used in a way that is not always straightforward, I will refer to what the Leader of the Opposition said about deficit reduction. Last Friday, the Leader of the Opposition indicated that there was a lack of consistency between what I said and what my colleague, the Minister of Finance, had said, saying that the GST would contribute to deficit reduction.
I would like to remind the hon. Leader of the Opposition that in the technical papers of August last it was written: "The GST will contribute to deficit reduction effort and ensure we can continue to pay for programs".
I go back to the December papers where it is written yet again:

-that the GST will contribute to the government's deficit-reduction effort and help us continue to finance, etc., the programs and services to which Canadians are attached.
So, Mr. Speaker, I note that the opposition members, especially the Liberals, brought this country's finances to a sort of dead end which we are trying to change, modify and improve. Instead of helping to solve the problem that they created, the members of that party systematically oppose for partisan reasons everything we suggest to reduce government spending and to improve economic efficiency.
The Leader of the Opposition just said that the GST was "a tax on consumption", a consumption tax. I gladly agree, because 48 countries have one. This type of tax in itself does not-
How many countries have two such taxes?

How many countries have 11 finance ministers? It won't kill us! There!
He said this tax would come down particularly hard on people on low and modest incomes. I repeat, we are going to replace a hidden tax that is slowly but surely destroying the economy with a modern tax. However, a consumer tax can be regressive unless it is accompanied by a certain number of measures. That is why we have put in place the best system-compared with all other countries that have this kind of value-added tax-to prevent and correct any regressive aspects of the sales tax, and I am referring to a system of tax credits-
Not indexed?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Not indexed!
Typical of our friends from Quebec, but we Acadians are used to being corrected this way!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
I believe the past bodes well for the future. In successive Budgets we have always adjusted our credits and we are committed to doing so in future as well.
In any case, there is a tax credit system. We have also eliminated a number of commodities on which people on modest incomes are most likely to spend, such as rent, drugs and food. As a result, we have a system that adequately protects families with incomes of $30,000 or less, so that after the tax reform they will have more money than they had before.
Of course the opposition knows taxes are not a popular subject and I realize that people would prefer not to pay taxes at all, which is a perfectly normal reaction. So they are concerned, and the opposition is playing on that concern and making outlandish statements that have no connection at all with the GST. To hear them you would think companies will collapse under the tax burden. Nobody would make money any more, and meanwhile, it seems, we would make a terrific profit. It doesn't make sense. Why should we want to bring our economy to a standstill when what we want to do is put it back on track?
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) said that although we were replacing the manufacturer's tax because it was a bad tax, we increased it by 50 per cent over a number of years. And so we did. We used mechanisms that had been in place for 64 years to collect the funds we needed to carry out government programs. However, we tried to find ways to replace this pernicious tax, and we identified a modem, equitable and fair approach that was not only necessary but long overdue. I believe the government is acting responsibly, and the opposition parties should realize how important it is to continue our efforts to put our financial house in order. They were largely responsible for putting this country's economy in a practically untenable situation in the first place. Since 1984, we have been working very hard to turn the situation around. The goods and services tax is a modem tax that protects people on low- and modest incomes and, I repeat, it is a tax that exists in 48 countries. When people say: Sure, but none of these countries has a federal system of government. If that is the only drawback, let's discuss it, but they go on to mention the rest. It will be 7 per cent more. That's not true. We are removing a 13.5 per cent tax to replace it with a broader tax of 7 per cent. Canadians and consumers will in the end pay the same amount they were paying before. It will be a much more dependable way of collecting the revenues the government needs, and it will protect our ability to provide government programs. All in all, I repeat, this is a necessary, advanced and equitable tax reform, and I am sure that increasingly, Canadians will come to understand this.

Mr. Speaker, the government's proposed good and services tax has sparked a great deal of intense debate in recent months. I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this issue that concerns and will potentially affect all Canadians. To state that I have serious apprehensions and misgivings regarding the GST would be an understatement.
I would like to outline some of the more troubling aspects of the proposed GST, with particular emphasis on those aspects that have the most effect on my province. I am convinced that the implementation of the GST will have serious detrimental effects on the citizens of Prince Edward Island and on all Canadians.
April 9, 1990

The government seems determined to implement the GST, despite the fact that approximately 80 per cent of Canadians disapprove of this new tax. It believes this is the time to implement this tax because it feels there will be enough time for people to forget before the next election. Instead of listening and responding to the concerns of the provinces, of businesses and of ordinary Canadians, the government is promoting the GST with an advertising campaign costing millions of dollars.
Canadians have every reason to be upset. Canadians are tired of the tax increases imposed on them since the Conservatives took power. From 1984 to 1988, personal income tax has increased by 106 per cent, corporate tax has increased by 49 per cent, and indirect taxes have increased by 54 per cent, and still there is very little reduction in the deficit.
A study done by the Canadian Council on Social Development says that taxes on the poor since 1984 have increased seven times those that are charged to the rich. Because of increases in personal and indirect taxes, the middle-income Canadian is now shouldering a disproportionate share of the tax burden. Not only are we paying more, we are receiving less. The GST will further aggravate this situation.
No one will argue that the manufacturers' sales tax is a tax that should be retained. No one will argue that this country does not need tax reform. No one will deny that we need a more simple and equitable tax system. But the GST is not tax reform. It is just a new tax, an unfair tax, an inflationary tax, a complicated tax which has all the earmarks of a bureaucratic horror show.
All Canadians will be affected by the inflationary impact of the GST. While the government expects only a 2.25 per cent increase in inflation by 1991, the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants predicts that this figure could be doubled as a result of the GST, which means that it will be 4.5 to 5 per cent. This coupled with the ordinary inflation, we will be experiencing a 10 per cent inflation figure by 1991.
Introduction of the GST in the present circumstances will create a two-tiered sales tax system in every province except Alberta. This will be chaotic for both business and consumer. Small business will be facing a
Government Orders
compliance nightmare and consumers will find themselves in a state of confusion at the retail counter.
We were promised a visible tax. Consumers would be aware of how much federal tax they would be paying. The Consumers Association of Canada feels that visibility is an essential principle of any tax change. Consumer awareness lends to greater political accountability, greater reluctance to bump up the tax rate at budget time, and fewer accusations of unfair pricing.
There is little doubt that the GST will contribute to the worsening of existing regional disparities. The impact of the GST will be most harmful in the provinces with the highest provincial tax rates. These high provincial taxes will be imposed after the GST has already been added to the cost of an item. That is, there will be a tax on a tax. Therefore, the proposed new tax system will have a particularly detrimental effect on provinces with high tax rates and those provinces tend to be the ones which already have weak economies.
In Prince Edward Island, there will be a total of 17 per cent charged through the GST and the provincial tax system. The 10 per cent provincial tax will be added to the cost of the item plus the cost of the GST.
Another very serious problem arising from the GST, and one that will further contribute to regional disparities, is the fact that the tax will apply to transportation. Transportation costs are a vital factor for all Canadians, but particularly for those who live in regions remote from the production and distribution centres.
For example, a farmer in Prince Edward Island will have to pay more for farm equipment than a farmer in Ontario because of the increased costs in transporting the finished product from the point of production. Moreover, the imposition of the GST will also affect fuel costs. Even though transportation companies will be able to claim back the GST paid on fuel, the finance department apparently plans to offset this revenue shortfall by raising excise taxes on fuel. This additional cost for transportation companies will be passed on to consumers in the form of higher rates.
Once again, the ultimate bearer of the new tax will be the consumer. It appears equally evident that the consumer who lives in remote and rural areas will suffer the

April 9, 1990
Government Orders
most from the increase in transportation costs. Atlantic Canadians will get it in the neck one more time.
It is time for a change. The government should be devoting its efforts to alleviating regional inequities rather than imposing a tax which will help keep the poor provinces poor.
The effects of the GST will vary from sector to sector. One of the industries that will be hardest hit by the GST is tourism. It is irresponsible for the government to push through a tax proposal that will seriously damage an industry that generates $24 billion in gross revenues per annum, that has created new jobs faster than any other sector, that is Canada's second largest earner of foreign exchange, and that generates $11 billion in tax revenue for all levels of government.
According to the Tourist Industry Association of Canada, the industry will lose $1 billion per year and 25,000 jobs by 1993, if the GST goes through. Moreover, many of the 60,000 small tourist enterprises will be placed in jeopardy.
The imposition of the GST will also raise the price of domestic air fares and domestic holiday tours. Canadians will be discouraged from taking vacations in their own country. This will be extremely harmful, since approximately 70 per cent of total tourist dollars is spent by Canadians in Canada. Tourists will be further deterred from taking their holidays in Canada by the fact that the cost of eating in restaurants will increase because of the goods and services tax.
The effects of the goods and services tax on tourism will be particularly devastating for the Atlantic provinces. About half of the tourists who visit these provinces are from central Canada. These tourists might find that, in light of the GST, a trip to the United States of America might be easier on the pocket-book.
According to the Canadian Tourist Research Institute, Prince Edward Island will suffer more than any other province because tourism makes up 10.5 per cent of Prince Edward Island's gross provincial product.
The agricultural and small business sectors will also be seriously affected by the proposed GST. Cash flow problems will be further aggravated. While many of the goods and services that are being used by a farmer will be taxed and rebated, the farmer will still be required to pay
the tax up front. Farmers will be forced to spend a lot of time and money figuring out the claims system and maintaining detailed records in order to comply.
According to John Bulloch of the CFIB, the ultimate compliance nightmare will be caused by the two-tiered tax system. The GST alone has to be accounted for at every stage of the production-distribution chain. The government's attempts to simplify the accounting procedures are, in Mr. Bulloch's words, "the most complex part of the whole nightmare". This is typical of the bureaucracy. By simplifying things, they make it more complex.
The complexity of the system will add significantly to accounting costs, not only for the business owners and farmers, but also for those who have to comply with a sales tax system for the first time.
For example, fishermen in Prince Edward Island who, for the most part have had their record keeping maintained for them by the large fish processing companies, will be faced with significant administrative costs when the GST is implemented. They will have to file monthly GST returns in order to be eligible for rebates on their purchases. The Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen in Atlantic Canada says that the fishery sector in Prince Edward Island will be particularly hard hit with high costs arising from the administration of the GST.
Another problem area that I would like to address briefly is housing. Flousing ownership was once regarded as an inalienable social right of Canadians. Past governments have instituted programs to help people save for a down payment. In 1985, this government killed the RHOSP. In 1990, the same government is adding GST costs which will help make home ownership even more unaffordable and will impact negatively on the construction industry. GST will also be added to legal fees, appraisal fees, real estate fees, et cetera, further inhibiting home ownership.
These are only a few of the burdens added to the tax load of Canadians by the goods and services tax. It is a terrible tax: inflationary, cumbersome, unfair and expensive to administrate. The GST is not the answer. I ask the government to withdraw it. Since Atlantic Canada is especially hard hit, I ask the Conservative members from
April 9, 1990

Atlantic Canada to live up to their responsibilities to the people of the region and join us in killing this odious tax.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today with firm resolve to speak as an Alberta member of Parliament and to speak on this measure at the report stage on legislation introducing the goods and services tax.
All Canadians are aware of the controversy in the debate generated by this aspect of tax reform. Of course, members of the opposition have not helped. They have played upon the natural fears of many Canadians through using misinformation, the only weapon they have in their arsenal.
This is, and will continue to be, a tough debate on the streets, in the coffee shops and over the kitchen table in homes across Canada. Some constituents have urged me to vote in favour of the GST and some constitutents have urged me to vote against the GST. What are the factors that I must consider? What are the arguments on either side? Let me deal first with why I should even consider voting against the GST. There are nine commonly cited reasons.
One, if the GST were a new tax raising buckets of new money for the federal government, then I should vote against the GST.
Two, if the GST were a cash cow easily increased once in place, then I should vote against the GST.
Three, if Albertans do not already pay a sales tax and we know that that is one of the ways that we as Albertans define ourselves, then I should vote against the GST.
Four, if the GST were to create a spiral of inflation in our economy, I would be the first on my feet to vote against it.
Five, if this were an unfair tax that hurt the poor and the seniors, then I should vote against the GST.
Six, if the GST were to be an administrative nightmare for small business and farmers, then I should vote against the GST.
Seven, if businesses and farmers would have to pay GST on their rent, on their equipment, on their supplies and other purchases resulting in an increase to input
Government Orders
costs, then I should vote against the GST. If the GST were to increase costs of production in agriculture, then I, as chair of the agricultural caucus representing a strongly agricultural riding, should vote against the GST.
Eight, if I felt the elimination of the existing federal sales tax would not be passed along to consumers, then I should oppose the GST.
Finally, number nine, if I felt there were several better alternatives or even one better alternative, then I would vote against the GST and call for that better alternative.
The bare facts do not sustain any of these propositions. Let us examine them one by one.
First, this is a replacement tax. The GST replaces the federal sales tax. Both the old FST and the new GST raise about $18 billion net for the Canadian treasury.
Second, if governments wanted a secret cash cow, they would keep the existing federal sales tax. Perhaps, this is the real reason that some members of the Liberals and the NDP oppose the GST. They want the so-called painless secret cash cow provided by the existing federal sales tax. The Conservative party wants an open and a visible tax so that Canadians know when they are paying for the services they receive from this government.
Three, Albertans already pay $1.7 billion in federal sales tax. Under the GST, they will pay about the same amount.
Four, regarding inflation, there is clear evidence from other countries that indicates that such a change does not create a spiral of inflation, because of the removal of the federal sales tax at the time that the new goods and services tax is introduced.
Five, regarding seniors and lower-income Canadians, the GST does not tax groceries, rent, health care and other basic necessities which compose the bulk of expenditures of these people.
Six, regarding administration for small business and for farmers, the GST tax return is but one page in length.
Seven, the GST will decrease input costs. For example, a farmer presently pays federal sales tax on the purchase of a pick-up. Under the GST, he or she will not be paying that input cost any more.
Eight, with respect to whether the eliminated FST will be passed on to consumers, we know that if one retailer

April 9, 1990
Government Orders
is slow to pass along the difference another will not be. That is the basis of economic competition in our society.
Finally, is there an alternative? Yes, Mr. Speaker, there are alternatives, but I can assure you that they are all worse in their impact on my riding, on my province, and on my country.
We could stay with the federal sales tax. We could continue to damage the economy and to eliminate thousands of jobs that never got a chance to get started. We could increase income tax. Is that what they want? They want us to increase income taxes. They want to increase other taxes. Or, we could cut out important programs like pensions. Is that what they want to do? There are always simple answers, and they do not work.
It is my view that I was not elected to simply be popular and to try to get re-elected. I believe that I was elected to make judgments and do the right thing for my riding, my province and my country. For these reasons and for many more, I will vote for the goods and services tax.

Mr. Speaker, the best of luck to that hon. member. We are going to see an alternative all right, an alternative sitting in that seat after the next election.
I want to begin my remarks by saying how disappointed and disgusted I am in witnessing this continual abuse of parliamentary procedure by the Conservative government. The government has decided again to invoke closure, or time allocation as it is properly called, on almost every piece of legislation in this House.
Since I was elected, the government has moved to limit debate no less than 37 times. That is more often than any government in history since Confederation. No wonder the Conservative government is at an all-time, precedent-setting, record low of 15 per cent in the polls, and going down. Read all about it. It states in the newspapers that no other Canadian government has fallen to such levels since Gallup began polling during the Second World War. Mr. Reid states that this is a signal that Canadians think the government is adrift. Adrift, Mr. Speaker!
I rise in support of the motions moved by my colleague for Gloucester, seconded by the member for Kingston and the Islands. The motions would have the effect of deleting the most substantive portions of the bill. These portions would have the effect of putting into law the concerns raised by the Official Opposition regarding the goods and services tax.
What are those concerns, Mr. Speaker? Permit me to list them for you: that the GST is regressive; that the GST is unfair; that the GST is inflationary; that the GST will be a nightmare to administer for the government and businesses. According to the Minister of National Revenue, the start-up costs for the GST alone will be over $1 billion and will cost over $380 million to administer every year.
The legislation before us would entrench a system of taxation that would put the tax burden squarely on the shoulders of the less well off in our society.
I could not help but listen to the two hon. members earlier. The member for Calgary Southeast had the audacity to ask: "What are they doing here?", referring to the opposition. He says that we are wasting time here in the highest court of the land. But I would like to remind that hon. member for Calgary Southeast that we in the opposition represent 80 per cent of Canadians on this issue. Eighty per cent of Canadians say no GST. I suppose that the hon. member for Calgary Southeast represents the remaining 20 per cent.
Then the member for Calgary Southeast had the nerve and the audacity to call the members for Calgary Northeast and Edmonton Southeast "characters". They are Members of Parliament. They are fellow caucus members of the member for Calgary Southeast. These gentlemen, and I suppose there are other members of Parliament in there as well, know best the demands and the wishes of their constituents. They are the ones who are there in the riding. Yet the member for Calgary Southeast has the nerve to stand up and call the members for Calgary Northeast and Edmonton Southeast characters just because they are acting in the best interests of their constituents. It is their constituents who are telling their member of Parliament, the person they gave the privilege and the honour to stand in this House, to say no to the GST because that is what the
April 9, 1990

constituents want them to do. The member for Calgary Southeast calls them characters and makes idle threats: "Kick them out of caucus", he says.
Even before this second stage of the tax reform had taken shape culminating in the bill before us, the Conservative government, led by the Prime Minister, managed to raise taxes 32 separate times since taking office in 1984. The present manufacturers' sales tax, a tax which the Minister of Finance called a silent killer of jobs, was raised by him from 9 per cent in 1984 to 13.5 per cent today. Each time he raised the tax, in essence he became an accomplice to the elimination of Canadian jobs. Under the second stage of tax reform-now, there is a word, "reform". The Tories did not want to call it what it really is, they call it tax reform. A good PR job sells it better-it is becoming increasingly clear that the poor and middle classes will be hit even harder with the GST. We have heard examples of that, especially from the hon. Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, the member for Windsor West. He gave all kinds of examples of how that tax is going to hit us along the way.
Under the second stage of tax reform, this government has forgotten, but it must recognize that whatever tax system is finally put in place it must promote fairness and eradicate economic discrimination. The GST is not such a tax. It would have the opposite effect and here are a few examples. The Hamilton and District Homebuilder's Association states that the GST will add $3,000 to the price of a new home. In Metro Toronto, this could be as high as $9,000.
Due to the GST, the government expects a minimum increase in inflation of 2.25 per cent. Of course, we know that is going to signal the Bank of Canada to maintain high interest rates, adding to the cost of a new home, car, or whatever other investments.
The Conference Board of Canada estimates that the number of jobs that will be lost due to the tax could be as high as 72,000 in 1991.
If the government has its way under the changes to the unemployment insurance system, Canadians who lose their jobs, through no fault of their own, will receive less entitlement for a shorter period of time.
The tax will be a nightmare for small businesses to administer. It could cost them over $2,000 in compliance costs alone. The Conservative Government had prom-
Govemment Orders
ised an annual subsidy for small businesses, but instead has opted for a one-time allowance.
The government has also placed the onus on businesses to decide whether or not they will include the GST on the shelf price of the good, or at the cash register. If they include the GST on the shelf price, the Minister of Finance says that businesses should post signs saying that the GST has been included. However, his officials have confirmed that there is no requirement to do so, meaning that another promise has been broken that the tax would be visible.
Let us not forget the provincial sales tax. Even though the provinces stand to gain, there will be a little windfall for the provinces in applying the GST then the provincial sales tax on top of the price of the good. So the Ontario Government, for example, stands to win. This government cannot get one province on board to help administer this tax.
Canadians should remember that included in the second stage of tax reform are massive cuts to existing programs. Some of these are familiar to Canadians already. The clawback on Old Age Security, the freeze on payments to Canada Assistance Plans for the needy, withdrawal of government support for the Unemployment Insurance Program. The GST is simply part of the over all Conservative strategy to paint a misleading picture of our present situation.
In closing, as a member of the Official Opposition, I respect the fact that Canadians can and should be encourage to join in pursuit of the free market. However, I do not believe that the operation of this country should be financed on the backs of those who are least capable of paying, which is what I believe is proposed in the GST.
For the record, GST simply means "government sanctioned theft".

Mr. Speaker, we are going to axe the tax and put in a tax that is fair.
The other day people opposing the goods and service tax decided to phone my office. I happened to be there and picked up the phone and talked to a Mrs. Carmichael. She told me how terrible this tax was. I said: "Mrs. Carmichael, we are going to axe the tax". And she said: "Oh, that is marvellous. You are going to axe the tax". I said: "We are going to axe the federal sales tax, Mrs. Carmichael". She said: "That is wonderful. Why didn't you say so?". Well, that is what I have been saying across

April 9, 1990
Government Orders
the country. That is what the whole policy is about. The policy is about getting rid of the most unfair, unCanadian piece of legislation that the government has had in force since 1924.
We have had report after report: three royal commissions. There was the Goodman study, on behalf of the hon. Marc Lalonde; a study undertaken by Mr. MacEa-chen, a study undertaken by Mr. Chretien; a study done by Mr. Turner; a study done by our present Minister of Finance; all designed to find out how they could alter the current federal sales tax and do something other than a goods and services value-added tax.
Time after time governments realized how wonderful the current tax was for them, because under this current tax when taxpayers' put their hands in their purses or wallets and take their money out, the government takes their money and they do not know it. We are going to axe that tax and we are going to put in a tax that is fair, visible, upfront, honest and works for the benefit of Canada.
It is regressive.

This tax covers the whole gambit of goods and services in the country. It is designed to be rebatable and take the burden off our industry and off our business. In the rebatable system what we do is allow business to invest in new buildings and new machinery and farms to buy new pick-up trucks, new milking machines and new things that they presently pay tax on and get that tax rebated to them so they can grow, develop, create and make a better Canada without the burden of tax on their backs. That is a 4 per cent refundable tax credit to every single developer-creator in Canada. That is what we are doing. We are building Canada.
My friends on the other side are worried about building Canada. They want to make sure that there is a weak, wimpy Canada because they are weak and wimpy.
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!

We are now at report stage of a bill that has had before it was engrossed a very thorough study across Canada by the finance committee. It has been the subject of a report. It has had a further study by the department that resulted in a bill which was brought before this House on second reading and then referred to the finance committee for further study and further amendment. A whole host of amendments were put through.
Two excellent amendments, by the way, were put by the hon. member for Essex-Windsor dealing with the benefits to credit unions and psychoanalysts, an exempt profession. These are good amendments that were put forward by the member for Essex-Windsor.
It is too bad members of the Official Opposition could not get around to doing any thinking on the bill because they too probably could have come up with some more amendments that were worth while. But, what did they do? Their amendments before us today simply say: axe this section, axe that section, get rid of that clause, get rid of the other clause, but there is nothing progressive, no creative thinking.
I recommend to the House tonight the amendments put forward by the hon. member for Mississauga West dealing with the horse racing industry and with the ability of charities and others to run bingos so that that kind of fund raising on behalf of charities bears no tax. These are the kinds of amendments that have come out of hard work done by members of this House in changing, persuading and ameliorating the problems of this tax to make it work better.
I want to thank members of the finance committee who worked on it, my colleagues from Mississauga West, from Essex-Windsor and others for the efforts in making the bill work the way it ought to work, because it is a pretty simple form of taxation.
I am told it is awfully complicated. I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, in a simplistic way all you have to do is put two nails on the wall. On the one nail, you put all the bills you received for everything you buy, and on the other nail put all the invoices you have for everything you sell. Then once every three months or once a month, depending on how often a small business wishes, they simply subtract one pile of bills from the other pile of bills, multiply by 6.54, and that is what they send in. That is as simple as you can get.
April 9, 1990
What about those who have nothing to sell?

If you have nothing to sell, you create nothing. Then you pay the tax because you are a consumer and consumers pay consumption taxes.
We have a philosophy of taxation on this side and that philosophy is: as far as income is concerned we ought to tax income, we ought to tax work, but not so much as to persuade people who work that it is not worth their while to work. That is why we have managed over a period of time to reduce our income tax rates. We have to do more of that, but we have reduced income tax rates as we did in stage one of tax reform.
We have to tax capital, but not so much as to make investment unfair or inappropriate. We have done that as we have worked, bit by bit, through amending the Income Tax Act and other statutes. Here we are reorganizing our consumption tax in such a way that we get growth in consumption tax activity instead of the negative attitudes that have been expressed in the existing federal sales tax. This tax creates a new growth attitude in Canada, a growth attitude of 1.4 per cent above the existing base case, that improves Canada and makes it bigger, grander, and finer.
It creates an additional $9 billion worth of new wealth in the second year of the tax and probably more. They say it is going to cost us $300 million in additional costs. I guess I would spend $3 to make $90 any day. That is what we are talking about when we talk about costs.
Where are we? We are in the final stages of a debate in this House of Commons to change a tax system that Canadians have been asking to have changed since the Rowell-Sirois report of 1940. No government has had enough guts, drive or initiative to do what has been necessary.
You do not rule by the Gallup poll. You do not govern by the Gallup poll. You govern by election, and we presented to the people of this country our alternative for sales tax reform in the White Paper of 1987. That White Paper formed the basis on which we went to the country in 1988, and the country endorsed this party as the government. It is on that endorsement that this policy is now before us here, in final form, endorsed by the people of Canada in the election of 1988.

Give us a break.
This is a simple form of taxation. Even Mr. Bulloch will be able to figure it out when he gets around to it.
Don't count on it.

My friend says "Don't count on it", but I have to say that even Mr. Bulloch will figure it out. Once it is in place I believe we will have the provinces of this country joining up in this tax system. Sure, it is unpopular now. Sure, we are unpopular, doing the tough things that have to be done, but we are trying to make Canada grow and we are building a nation. We are not building a society of wimps and weasels, and wastrels.

Mr. Speaker, it is an unexpected pleasure to be able to speak after the hon. member for Mississauga South. As I listened to him I knew I was listening to someone who was so absolutely out of touch with the Canadian people that he could say that public dissatisfaction with this GST is actually diminishing. The member is radically and completely out of touch with the Canadian people. Of course the tax is unpopular. Any tax is bound to be unpopular. It is not a question of whether the tax is in itself is unpopular, because obviously there is a natural tendency for tax to be unpopular.
However this particular tax is unpopular for a deep and fundamental reason. The member fails to read history. What history says is that over and over again governments, administrations and regimes that fail to listen bring in a tax which cracks the system and forces change. Every major revolution over the last 200 years or 300 years has been triggered by an unpopular and unnecessary tax. I suspect, unless this government listens more carefully in the hours, weeks and months ahead, what we are seeing now is a fundamental radical realteration of the Canadian political landscape.
I spent last weekend in my home constituency, as did most members. In Victoria I was impressed not only with the amount of the opposition to the GST but the underlying sense of bitterness and despair that we have a government in Canada that simply will not listen to the Canadian people. This government has learned as a result of the 1988 election a mistaken lesson. It learned

April 9, 1990
Government Orders
then that it could recover from unpopularity if it just hung in there.
It is now trying to apply that lesson to the current situation. It has been advised by tax advisors who simply fail to understand that a tax system is an intricate system of social economic relationships. To tinker in a fundamental way as this tax does is to set loose major tremors through the whole economic system at a time when the Canadian economy simply cannot take it. For example, the government and its advisors, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister have said over and over again that this tax will not be inflationary. They have studies to prove it. Already the people are understanding more than the government knows, that this tax is going to be dramatically inflationary at a time in our economy when we cannot stand it.
I have a tax notice that a senior citizen received in Victoria. The tax notice is for a tax increase of 17 per cent that comes into force on July 1 of this year. The landlord, in explaining the tax increase, says it is because of the GST. We know that workers across this country are beginning to gear their wage demands to take into account the effect of inflation. We know that prices are already beginning to be jacked up in anticipation of the GST. Real estate prices are going up in anticipation of the GST. The people know that this tax is going to be inflationary.
Why won't the government listen? This weekend we had what was called the no campaign. People had an opportunity in more than 500 communities across Canada to vote on the GST. Certainly in Victoria they came out in amazing numbers. People of all persuasions, of all points of view, were united around a single clear message, and that is no to the GST. As I emphasized before, it is not simply a reaction to being taxed more. When one has a chance to sit and chat carefully with the people who are signing these cards, one uncovered a range of attitudes. In some cases it was a negative feeling toward any increased taxation. In many cases it was thoughtful, careful business people who have studied this and who are worried and afraid of the impact of this tax on their business and the administrative chaos that is going to ensue.
I talked to a couple who are involved in the clothing business in Victoria and Vancouver. They already find
that the retail prices in Washington, just south of the border, equal their wholesale prices. They worry about what the GST will do to them.
There was another couple who had a business. They looked into the administrative aspects of this and found there were tremendous complications in collection that this is going to cause. Another man has been a Conservative all his life. He was feeling a sense of tension and anxiety at the cheating that he says will happen in his particular business. He does not want to do that. He says that, in competition, he is going to be forced to do that, or he is going to be forced out of business.
These are genuine concerns. They are based on life-long experience and this government should listen. There will be hundreds of thousands of Canadians over this weekend who will sign these cards. They will take the special effort of signing a card and filing it, and asking the government to say no to the GST. It is not too late for the government to listen.
I suggest that in mere self-preservation the government must begin to listen to the people of Canada. The member for Mississauga South made a virtue of acting in the face of public opinion polls, and certainly there are circumstances under which those acts of political courage are necessary. But this is an act of arrogance and foolhardiness, pushing forward with this tax in the face of the collective wisdom of the Canadian people.
It is now very clear that the impact of this tax is felt most strongly among those who have spent their lives as Conservatives, who have been supporters through thick and thin of this Conservative party. It is ironic that it is the Conservative party which is now seen by so many people as leading this country into disintegration and disarray. This was the party that founded Canada in many respects, that had that initial, historic vision.
It is now the party that is perceived by many of its own supporters as dividing and causing the disintegration of this country. We have the free trade agreement. We have the litany that we have been raising in this House over the last number of months; the disintegration of social programs, unemployment insurance, seniors' programs. We have had in recent months and weeks the elimination of funding for women's programs, a clear and absolute violation of the responsibility of this government.
April 9, 1990

Now we find that this party, which was elected back in 1957 and 1958 on the campaign for the freedom of Parliament and against closure, has used closure to impose this unpopular, unfair, dishonest tax on the Canadian people. The GST is part of the Americanization of Canada. The government is refusing to see that we have, in this country, a distinctive social and economic system which needs changing in a different way than that the government takes us.
This government moves us increasingly into an integration with the American economy. We must have a tax system that reflects the essential social democracy of this country which is fair, honest and open. The government's refusal to listen to the Canadian people will mean the end of a Canadian institution. I must say I do not spend too much time worrying about the fate of the Conservative party, but it is an institution which has played a part in keeping this country together.
What is happening in Victoria is happening in community after community across the country. The Reform Party for example, in my riding, has now signed up 800 members. Clearly, from the impression I had on the weekend, it has replaced the Conservative party as the voice of conservativism in western Canada.
That means that western Canada is now represented by a sectarian party which does not and cannot properly represent all Canadians. But it is a symptom of the disease which has been inflicted on this country by the Conservative party.
I call on the House to reject this bill, to reject this tax and I call on the government to pause once before it crosses the brink. It is not too late. The Canadian people must be listened to. The Canadian people will be listened to.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have an opportunity to participate in what I hope is near the end of a lengthy process of reforming the tax system which this government began about five years ago. I have been part of that process for most of that time. Over the course of that time we have seen more misinformation, hysteria and nonsense on this subject than perhaps any other that has ever been

discussed, with the possible exception of the free trade debate during the last election campaign.
I took the time yesterday to find one of the tabloids that I used in the last election campaign because I wanted to make sure that what I was doing here on this subject was consistent with what I was doing in the election campaign. I took that tabloid out. I have it here and it has a nice picture of me and one of the Prime Minister and some senior citizens. It talks about free trade and has some information about that. But what is important is what is on the back here-
Show us what is on the back. There is another picture there too.
That is right. There is another picture. There is a picture of myself and the Minister of Finance. He was the Minister of Finance then and he is now.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is referring to a picture album of himself. Since that is a document to which he is referring, I would ask that it be tabled for the benefit of other members of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Edmonton Northwest has the floor.
Mr. Speaker, I would be more than glad to table it. But before I table it I will quote something from it. It talks about tax reform. It says the following.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: First, the hon. member will not be able to table it. Second, I would appreciate if he would just leave it on his desk and quote from it there.

Mr. Speaker, I will be glad to do that. What I said in that document was that tax reform is an issue in this election. That of course was the last election. We had completed the first stage which was income tax reform, corporate and personal. I was talking about the second stage of tax reform because we had completed the first stage:

April 9, 1990
Government Orders
The second stage of tax reform will be the development of a better and fairer sales tax regime. The inadequacies of the present federal sales tax system are widely recognized; it is complex, hidden, unfair to lower-income Canadians, impedes the ability of Canadian firms to compete internationally, and is too narrowly-based. The present tax applies to only about one-third of the goods and services produced in Canada.
Changing the federal tax system is a very complex process. This government is committed to developing and implementing sales tax changes in full consultation with the provinces, the business community and individual Canadians. The government is continuing to work with the provinces-
Reform of the sales tax system will ensure that the revenue obtained will replace those of the old manufacturers' sales tax and will be accompanied by a significantly enriched sales tax credit-It will be designed to reduce the complexity, ensure the fair treatment of all businesses and eliminate both the inequities and competitive disadvantages that are a basic part of the current tax regime.
The government is also committed to ensuring that municipalities, hospitals, school boards, colleges and universities will not bear a greater tax burden under the new system and that basic groceries, prescription drugs and certain medical devices will not be subject to tax.
Those were my comments during the election campaign. I distributed 40,000 copies of that document in my constituency. I gave every elector in my constituency an opportunity to see what we were planning to do when we returned to office, as we were, because the people chose wisely and they recognized that this was a government with a platform, plan and vision.
What we are doing here today is implementing exactly what we said we were going to do in the last election campaign, exactly what I said we were going to do as stated in 40,000 copies of a tabloid that I distributed throughout my constituency.
Over the course of the last several months, we have heard from a lot of people who have talked about this particular tax. I would just like to let you know what some of them have had to say. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce said:
We do not favour the maintenance of the current manufacturers' sales tax. Its serious flaws have been well documented and need not be repeated here. We do support 1he concept of a value-added tax as a vehicle that could serve as the best replacement mechanism -
Some people might be interested to hear what Shirley Carr of the Canadian Labour Congress had to say. She said:
I should add that the Canadian Labour Congress has long been critical of the existing federal sales tax which is hidden, unfair, and economically destructive tax.
She was accompanied by Bob Baldwin, director of technical services. Ele said:
Within the realm of multi-stage taxes, there are all kinds of design options-We have not said we are opposing multi-stage taxes in principle.
Maybe we should talk about Mr. Bulloch because he had some things to say. Some members were quoting him earlier. I asked Mr. Bulloch the question: "Do you agree there is a problem with the existing federal sales tax that needs to be resolved? Is that true?". He said: "Yes". Then he said: "Everybody out there would like to have an alternative to a multi-stage sales tax. The trouble is, one is not out there".
Let us hear what some other people had to say. Mr. Alasdair McKichan, president of the Retail Council of Canada said:
Our members are firmly of the opinion that the current MST is outmoded and inefficient in a great many ways. We acknowledge it must be replaced and that the economy and the revenue needs of the government would best be served by a comprehensive goods and services tax along the lines of the type we are now considering.
I will give another example. Mr. Michael Geller, president of the Urban Development Institute said:
Our position is that the sales tax reform is necessary to reduce the deficit, to improve the over-all fairness of the tax system, and to ensure that Canada can compete effectively in the world. We will support a GST which will contribute to the realization of these goals.
Because there are many members who have automotive plants in their ridings, I will quote Mr. T. Mezon, Government Relations Committee of the Automotive Industries Association of Canada:
As a representative of the manufacturing sector of our association, let me say that we are in agreement with the proposed GST We think that the current FST has been an unfair burden for the Canadian manufacturer.
Mr. Roy M. Woodbridge, president of the Canadian Advanced Technology Association said:
I can tell you pretty categorically that if you got a roomful of our members and asked them, taking the good and the bad all together, how many are in favour of this, you would have about 98 percent raising their hands in favour.
I could go on and on because I have a long list here, but I know that I am out of time, so I will thank you and allow the next speaker to continue.
April 9, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight, and it is night, it is six o'clock and supper hour, to say that I am against Bill C-62 and will vote against it. Every consumer sitting around their kitchen table can say that the food on that table will not be taxed because it is a necessity. But next year every consumer in Canada will pay an additional 7 per cent on everything else in the kitchen.
The minister can talk about his 13.5 per cent-maybe he thinks he can fool some Canadians, but obviously he has not fooled 80 per cent of Canadians. The manufacturers' sales tax, or the federal sales tax, as the minister should be aware, is only on some goods. I do not say that it was a good tax. But I certainly do not think that the goods and service tax is a good tax when you think that everybody is going to pay 7 per cent on all goods and services, except on basic necessities such as food and medicine.
There are several reasons why I dislike this tax. One, it is regressive. It makes the lower income Canadians pay. I think there are other areas where this government could have looked to reclaim some money from Canadians- but I will come to that. It affects every low income Canadian, whether they are a student, unemployed, a widow, or single woman or man in their 50s, everybody. It means they will have to find 7 per cent more next year to buy the same thing that they bought with their income this year, except for some of the major items such as a car and they are still going to have to pay 7 per cent on a car.
The other thing is that it is inflationary. We are asking the people to find 7 per cent more in their income. It means higher wages and it also means, in my opinion, fewer jobs. There will be less incentive to buy come the beginning of the year until people get used to this tax. Next year they will need more money to do what they did this year.
The government says: "Oh, well, we are giving a credit to Canadians". I agree, they are giving a credit to Canadians. There has been a federal sales tax credit in the income tax system for the last three years. I have never heard statistics on how many Canadians filed income tax returns when they did not pay income tax nor have to pay income tax. I can only say that my constituency offices have many people who have never had to fill out an income tax return, and there are many people
Government Orders
who not even know that that credit has been there for the last three income tax years. As well, it means they must file an income tax credit in order to start receiving the credit next December. That means every Canadian.
It would be very amazing to me, a politician, to think that every Canadian will have enough awareness to know that they must file that income tax return in order to qualify for that credit. It takes a long time for people to get used to it. There is always an injury to Canadians until they get used it.
That's right.

The collection from the individual taxpayer is one thing but there is another element. It is only partially indexed. The National Council on Social Welfare estimates that a partial indexation of the goods and service tax credit will result in 100,000 families losing the credit within two years, and some 700,000 within five years. The Canadian Tax Journal tells us that 46 per cent of Canadian families earning less than $30,000 will pay more taxes in 1991, contrary to the government's argument as to the fairness of the goods and service tax.
The Minister of Finance says it will increase inflation by a factor of 1.25 per cent. That is his statistic. That is a government statistic. Many economists say that that is a very optimistic figure.
I see many other consequences that we do not have time to talk about here. I do know that next January there will be more bartering among people, and I cannot say that I am against it. Why not avoid the 7 per cent? Why not allow the poor or lower income Canadians to barter? I am certain that the higher income Canadians will go to the United States for services and the government will not get the 7 per cent. Why do I say that? If I were going to plan a trip to the United States, I would write to an American travel agency rather than pay the 7 per cent here for the same service. With the free trade agreement it could not be prevented because the United States would tell us that we were interfering with their way of work. I can see many areas where the government will lose the benefit of passing this goods and services tax.
I know we are under a 10 minute rule for speeches under closure and this is one of the last times to debate this bill. Tomorrow night at this time we will be voting on third reading. Contrary to what 80 per cent of Canadians may feel, by tomorrow night at this time the House will

April 9, 1990
Government Orders
not have the power to change anything in that bill unless it is returned to us from the Senate.
I say to the 80 per cent of Canadians, as a person who understands politics, there is only one way to make your voice heard between now and tomorrow night. My constituents have certainly written to tell me they are against the goods and services tax. I can only say to them, find the telephone number of your member of Parliament. Find out where his or her office is and make sure you report your feelings on the goods and services tax.
All weekend I heard: "Well, if 80 per cent of Canadians are against it, how can it pass?" It is a very real thing in our parliamentary system that we have a government which has a majority and the majority is going to pass this bill.
We have heard why it is a simple tax and why there are no other alternatives the government has wanted to look at, and I will get to those alternatives if I have a minute. I tell the Canadian people that a majority means that regardless of the feelings of constituents the government is going to pass this 7 per cent tax. I can only say to Canadians, get on the phone, go visit your MP's office by tomorrow night at six o'clock, and register your concern in their offices, at their desks.
Hear, hear!
That is your last chance-except of course in the next election. It can easily be done at that time but it is better to do it now so that the tax is not put into place.
The electorate will remember.

What are the alternatives? The government could have kept the federal sales tax, or it could have done away with it as people have said. It could have used the our income tax system as it is today by increasing the income tax levels of the three groups. But the government does not want to do that. It wants to bring in a 7 per cent consumption tax, a regressive tax. It could have gone to the single tax-as my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood has said- which has a lot of support across Canada from both businesses and economists. It could have closed existing loopholes, such as changing the capital cost allowance, as I have said before, so that it reflects a true replacement
cost. It could tax real capital income including capital gains.
At least these would be affecting the higher income earners rather than the lower income and the poor people of Canada. It could have gone after the business meals and entertainment deduction that tax specialists have said is a big loophole, a billion dollar loophole and growing.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that my time is ending and that I have two minutes.
I want to get very parochial because as a maritimer, as an Atlantic Canadian, a Canadian coming from the eastern part of Canada, there are other things that this tax does. It will affect our tourism trade.
Will it ever!

Yes, they can get a refund as they leave the country, but 7 per cent on top of everything else is very negative to tourists coming to Canada. It is certainly a better thing for the Canadians to go to the United States and not have to pay the 7 per cent on the goods and services there. I am sure there will be an exchange of tourism, but we will be going to the United States to buy instead of paying the tax here.
The other thing it does is to put a negative on transporting goods from the east to the Ontario market. We are going to have to add on an additional 7 per cent to our transportations costs, which in light of some of the things that have happened in the past few months, have gone up.
I know that my time has run out. I thank you for your endurance. I would only say that I think the government should reflect hard and long before bringing this bill in for third reading tomorrow. I think that the people in Canada should get busy and tell their representatives that they have a majority and they are abusing it.

speakeroldname: Hon. William C. Winegard (Minister for Science):
speakerposition: Minister for Science
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to participate in this debate today because I think it is important that we set this particular item in the context of what the government has been doing for the last several years.
We know that one of the difficulties facing Canada is that we may not be competitive down the road. If we look at what this government has tried to do over the last five
April 9, 1990

and a half years, most of those actions have been designed to make Canada a competitive country so we could enjoy the social programs that we all desire.
Take for example, the Foreign Investment Review Act.
Take it, please!

speakerposition: Minister for Science
speechtext: People said: "You have got to watch that. Don't let any of that foreign money in."
We've sold the country. Let it go.

speakerposition: Minister for Science
speechtext:
FIRA has gone, and the reason FIRA has gone is that we want to make Canada competitive. We welcome foreign capital.
Another example is the National Energy Program. I often hear what a marvellous thing the National Energy Program was for my province of Ontario. We know what damage it did to the west, but it also severely damaged my own province of Ontario. Let me explain. It damaged it because with the cheap energy, lower than world prices, Ontario industry became lazy. Ontario industry did not have to use their heads because they had the option of cheap energy. That was no favour to my province. The National Energy Program was bad for the whole country. That is why we got rid of it, to make Canada competitive.
With the free trade agreement, people wanted to draw the wagons around in a circle. They would prefer to have us trade only interprovincially. They did not want to have us get out and trade with the rest of the world. They said it would cost us jobs, and it would be terrible. The fact is that since it came in, 200,000-odd jobs have been created since January of 1989. Of course, they are not all due to the free trade agreement, but the net result has been positive.
We look at some of the other things that this government has tried to do. With deregulation we are trying to make Canada competitive with the rest of the world, and that is really what the GST is all about. When you have a 13.5 per cent manufacturers' sales tax, a tax that hurts Canadian industry and everyone agrees in this House that that is a bad tax-
Not as bad as the GST.

speakerposition: Minister for Science
speechtext:
-then you have to do something about it. When you have 22,000 exemptions to the current federal sales tax, you have to do something about it.
Government Orders
When your exemptions complicate the issue so much that you really do not know which way you are going, left or right, you had better do something about it. When you look at what we have in terms of our exports, every export in this country is penalized because of the current manufacturers' sales tax. The rate is somewhere perhaps between 1 per cent and 3 per cent. People say: "Well, if you are only penalizing your exports by 1 per cent or 3 per cent, what is that?" That represents something between 10 and 30 per cent of the total profit that the exporters are dealing with. That is another reason why you have to get rid of the manufacturers' sales tax.
There is a company in Guelph that operates a manufacturing section as well as an import section. The president of that corporation says to me: "Why would you continue with the current system? All you do is penalize me for manufacturing in Canada, because when I move to import things, I do not have to charge on that price for the sales tax, my distribution system, my importing system, and all those things. It is easier for me to import than it is to manufacture, so we have got to get rid of the manufacturers' sales tax."
Most people in this House have said over the past few days that they would like to get rid of the manufacturers' sales tax. We have had it for 64 years and we all recognize it is doing us damage. We have had the royal commissions and we have had statements by governments over the last 40 years about it but we have not done anything. How long do we go on putting something off that decreases the fundamental thing we need in Canada, namely, being competitive?
That is the thrust of most of the things that this government has tried to do. We are taking one more step in getting rid of those things that get in the way of making Canada a truly competitive trading nation. From all the things that were said during the free trade debate and those things that have been said in this House over the last several days we must enhance our trading position or we will not have the things that Canadians want.
We have got to get rid of the manufacturers' sales tax. No one questions that now, not even the members of the opposition but that is where the agreement stops. They would like something different. They say it is a tax that other people do not have.

April 9, 1990
Government Orders
We did not say we didn't have it; we said we didn't want it.

speakerposition: Minister for Science
speechtext:
There are 49 other countries in the world that have this goods and services tax. If this is such a terribly regressive tax why do those other countries manage to do quite well with it?
I heard one of my colleagues on the other side of the House talk about tourism and how bad it is for tourism. You had better tell some of the countries in Europe that. Obviously they do not understand it because their tourism is doing quite well and they all have the goods and services tax. There are 49 other countries, Mr. Speaker, with this tax.
And there are riots in Britain, riots in the streets.

speakerposition: Minister for Science
speechtext:
I have heard some of my colleagues on the other side say: "Whack it to them in income tax." They do not understand how much income tax would have to go up if that were done. That would again drive people out of this country, the people who are trying to put their money in to make the country go. I hear them say: "Oh, well, if you would tax the corporations more! Why do you not sock it to the corporations more?" We have done a lot of that over the last several years.
You heard the Minister of State for Finance talking today about the things we have done in terms of removing some of the tax loopholes which were used by corporations. We will continue to look at all those things.
What some of the opposition members really want is to sock the corporations so that they become uncompetitive with the rest of the world.
Tax the poor!

speakerposition: Minister for Science
speechtext:
That makes no sense. They want to drive the wealth-makers out. They do not understand how you create wealth. You create wealth by having corporations do new things, make new products and bring more funding into Canada. They do not understand that. All they understand is killing the corporations because they are nice things to attack. Corporations are not really people so you attack the corporations. If we drive the corporations out of Canada then we will not have the wealth that we all want, to have a Canada such as we really want.
I have heard that they want to talk about capital gains. Let's hit all those capital gains. What this government has done is put a limit on capital gains. It has also changed the rate at which capital gains are charged in terms of tax remittance. I do not think we should go any further. If you do not allow people who want to take a risk with their money to have some benefit from that, then you are not going to have the risk-takers in Canada. You will have the people who want to sit on their hands and clip their coupons and that is not going to do us any good. You have to have risk-takers. You do not have risk-takers if you don't let them keep something of what they take the risk for. But no. I know all my colleagues want to share the wealth-I know whose wealth they want to share. They want to share the wealth of the risk-takers and yet they do not want to take the risk themselves.
I have heard about this tax being regressive and terrible. A GST that exempts basic groceries, a GST that exempts residential rents is not a regressive tax when you then give back to the lower-income groups in the form of a tax credit that differential that they are going to have to pay.
One of the things we will do is make sure people apply-
If they apply.

speakerposition: Minister for Science
speechtext: -because we will have the advertising and will put slips in with their Old Age Security envelopes to say: "Please apply to do this". Listen to the beasts when we do. They will say: "You are advertising. You are doing terrible things". We will inform the people of this country about what they need to do to have their tax credit.
So will we.

speakerposition: Minister for Science
speechtext:
They are already getting their tax credit and they will get a larger one. So this tax is not, I repeat, not a regressive tax.
Some people tell me that the 13.5 per cent will not come off. They are living in a different world than I am. The competition that is coming from the free trade agreement, the competition coming from Europe '92 will ensure that corporations which do not take it off will not be in business. It will be as simple as that. But we also have the Department of Consumer and Corporate
