Affairs doing its very best to ensure that people are notified if the tax does not come off.
John Diefenbaker would not like this tax.

speakerposition: Minister for Science
speechtext: I have spoken to both the President of General Motors and the President of Ford. They can hardly wait until this is law so they can reduce their prices. That is exactly what they want to do, so they can compete better with others.
So they can reduce their costs.

speakerposition: Minister for Science
speechtext: As the Prime Minister said the other day: "We could take the easy way out. We could take the way out that every government has done for years, do nothing." We do not intend to do that. We intend to make Canada a competitive country. This is one more block in our story to do that.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to participate in the debate on the amendments that are before us, most of which were put to this House by our finance critic, the member from Gloucester. The hon. member has worked very diligently, not just on behalf of the members of this caucus, but on behalf of all Canadians, in trying to show this government the folly of its ways in this piece of political nonsense called the goods and services tax.
This particular group of amendments that have been put in this piece of legislation should be worthy of considerable debate. They were worthy of considerable debate in the committee studying this piece of legislation.
Once again, I find myself rising and speaking on behalf of over 80 per cent of Canadians. I think it is probably 87 per cent today. We know it is at least 85 per cent. If you take 100 and take the 15 per cent of Canadians who now support the Conservative party, you are left with at least 85 per cent that do not. I would suspect that those 85 per cent have seen the error of the ways of this government and have decided that they can no longer support it no matter where they live in this country because of the government's arrogant fiscal policies it has tried to foist upon the Canadian public.
The debate tonight on these amendments is limited. We know the Canadian public wants to see a full and thorough debate on this piece of legislation. This piece of legislation is singularly the most unpopular piece of legislation ever foisted upon the Canadian public by its
Government Orders
own government. It is a crazy piece of legislation. The government will see the next time it goes to the electorate that it will pay the price for not listening to the Canadian public.
In the report stage of this legislation, we have seen the government do what it has done at every stage of debate on this legislation. It has imposed time allocation. This government has imposed time allocation, over and over and over again, for fear that the more opposition members stand up here and speak on behalf of the majority of Canadians, the 85 or 87 per cent that are saying no to this GST, that there will be more members opposite who will wake up and smell the roses, listen to their constituents and do what they are elected to do, namely, to represent the views and interests of their constituents.
We have already seen what happens when you have freedom of thought and free expression on the other side. You get kicked out of certain rooms and certain caucuses to sit by yourself.
I want to submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that this particular piece of legislation that we are debating at report stage today is a piece of legislation that Canadians have decided must not, and will not, go through.
I have travelled this country from coast to coast. On one particular day I stood at the ferry terminal in Dartmouth on the Atlantic Ocean and saw over 2,000 individuals who told me that they wanted me to come to this place and tell this government "no" to this goods and services tax.
That very afternoon I was in the city of Calgary-Tory country. I talked to people in Calgary who had never voted anything but Progressive Conservative in their lives. They told me that they would never, ever, vote- their right arm would fall off before they would vote -for these people opposite because they felt betrayed. They felt betrayed because this government had put a policy in effect or tried to called the goods and services tax, which is completely contrary to their wishes, and what they said was completely contrary to even Tory philosophy.
Later that afternoon I was in downtown Vancouver. There, I stood shoulder to shoulder with Canadians from various parts of British Columbia who were collecting names on a petition, to try to show this government the

April 9, 1990
Government Orders
folly of its ways, to say no to the goods and services tax, but this government has not yet listened.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, after the government picked up the paper today and saw that it is the most unpopular government in the history of this country, it is going to have to start listening to Canadians.
The goods and services tax is not the only bad piece of fiscal policy that this government has tried to foist upon Canadians. This is perhaps the straw that broke the proverbial camel's back. In the last number of years we have seen a government that talked about tax fairness, sacred trust, and social policy over and over again, flip-flop on its positions on fiscal and social policy.
Do not forget, Mr. Speaker, that this is the government that partly de-indexed the old age pensions. I saw the Deputy Prime Minister in the Chamber a few minutes ago. He was the very man who stood up and said that the government supported a strong national railway from coast to coast. These are the very people who have dismembered our national railway from coast to coast in this country. They destroyed the national railway system when they dismembered VIA Rail.
This is the government that talked such a good game about regional development. The Prime Minister made much to do about nothing-now we find out-when he announced $1.05 billion for ACOA. Subsequent to that and subsequent to November, 1988, we saw this government completely withdraw its support and commitment. It is an age-old commitment that governments in Canada have given to regional development.
We have seen a government which has mismanaged not just the fisheries- I get up all the time, as do my colleagues, trying to shake some sense into those people opposite about the fisheries-but it has also mismanaged its agricultural sector into a state of complete chaos and collapse.
This is the government that talked about how consensus-building could work. This is the very government that went and told the poorest provinces of this country that they could not get what it expected from Established Programs Financing; the very funds that provinces like Nova Scotia, Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island rely on for their national
standards; for post-secondary educational institutions and health care. This is the government that did that.
This is the government that in the last budget lost all sense of propriety and withdrew funding that subsequently shut down women's centres from coast to coast in this country. This is the very government that used to have its Minister of State for Indian and Northern Affairs stand up and talk about all the wonderful things it was doing for aboriginal communities. Yet in this budget it cut the very funding for Native Friendship Centres from coast to coast.
And newspapers.

This is the government that has come forward and devastated veterans programs. There is nothing sacred any more. Everybody and every group is a target. This government does not know where to stop in its crazy pursuit of trying to get hold of its fiscal house because it does not know where it is heading and it does not know where it is coming from.
These are the very people that were telling seniors; "No, you are not the senior veterans who need those special programs for veterans affairs to help with their cleaning in the house". It is telling them now: "You must bear a disproportionate share of the burden that we have created as a Conservative government when we doubled your national debt between 1984 and 1989".
This is the very government that said it had a spending commitment, a spending priority, and that the funds were committed for a national system of child care from coast to coast in the country. The day after the electorate put its faith in this government, it flip-flopped and decided that it was not going to have a national child care program.
This is the government that went in 1984 to the Canadian electorate and said to those men and women who serve and have served this country greatly in international defence forces that it supported the national armed forces of the country and that it recognized the commitment of those men and women. The government came into this Chamber with a White Paper on defence and, as soon as the electorate got suckered into giving it
April 9, 1990

another term in office, it completely gutted the White Paper. It closed bases from coast to coast.
Not only that, but how many times in debate did we hear about the Polar 8 ice-breaker? It was on, and then it was changed. Then it was modified, and then it was put off. Not even the protestations of the member for Capilano-Howe Sound, who is the Associate Minister of National Defence, and the tears she could cry, could show the government the error of its ways. It cancelled that program as well.
On 33 occasions the government has come into this place and raised taxes for Canadians. It came in with a goods and services tax that it pretends is going to be revenue neutral. It pretends it is going to be simple. It pretends it is going to be fair. It pretends it is going to be single tiered.
The Prime Minister, when he is faced with 85 per cent opposition and 15 per cent standing in the polls, shows his typical arrogance in standing in the House, I believe he did it today, and saying: "Well we know that we are doing the right thing. What counts is what the votes are on election day."
What is going to count for the Prime Minister is what he is going to do after the next election outside politics. The Canadian people have placed their trust in this government's capabilities to manage the affairs of the country and to live up to their promises for the last time. The history books will record that the goods and services tax, this regressive tax, this assault on the wallets of the Canadian taxpayers, was the final nail in the coffin of the Mulroney government.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in the debate today.
The member who just spoke talked about how he was going to talk about all those amendments that members of the Liberal Party has proposed to this legislation so that they could improve it because they did not like it. He talked about everything but, and I guess that is why he is called the member from Dartmouth: because he has used his mouth to dart all over the place but he did not talk about the legislation itself. I find that rather disturbing because I think he should have.
Not only did he not talk about the legislation that is in front of us today, but I listened to other members make their pitches on the legislation. They said what they like
Government Orders
about it and what they did not like about it. Again, we have had some very good comments from some members of the House and some comments that are, if I might say, misleading from others.
This morning before I came to Ottawa I met with a group of seniors in my riding. There were about 25 of them. They probably reflect many of the same opinions as many seniors across Canada. They reflected opinions based on information that had been given to them to a degree by people in opposition who chose to give them the wrong information. Therefore, naturally, there are 85 per cent of Canadians opposed to it. I am surprised, with the information out there from those in opposition, that it is not 90 per cent or 95 per cent of Canadians opposed to the legislation.
I watched the debates here in the House. I would like to give you some examples, Mr. Speaker, of some of the things that have been said.
The member for Hamilton West chastised the government because the legislation did not require visibility of the tax. I take it he is not upset with the 7 per cent. He is not upset with all the contents of the tax. He just does not like it because it is not visible. Either he has not read the legislation or he needs an explanation.
I will give him the explanation so that he can very clearly understand what the legislation states. In fact Bill C-62 requires that the vendor-the store or shopkeeper, the business or whoever-must clearly indicate to the purchaser that the tax is included in its price. It must indicate 7 per cent in a sign or some mechanism somewhere in the store or, second, the actual amount of the tax has to be shown. That is in the legislation, and it is exactly opposite to the comments being expressed by that member. What that member wants us to do is: he wants us to go to the small business community, that community that he feels his party supposedly represents, that community that Mr. Bulloch represents, and force all those small businesses, those small mom and pop shops, those people who have small cash registers, to buy new cash register equipment. He wants us to force them to buy new point of sale equipment. He wants us to force them to go to IBM and buy those deluxe computers that really are not necessary because under our system of GST, under the legislation that we have, we are allowing businesses some freedom to indicate to their customers exactly how the tax is being applied.

Jean Colbert, a 17th century French statesman, once said that the art of taxation consists of plucking the goose so as to obtain the most feathers with the least amount of hissing.
While this and previous governments have returned again and again to pluck yet a few more feathers, our Canadian goose has traditionally protested little. It would honk about and flap a little bit just to let the government know that it would not be taken for granted, but the protest was generally short-lived and soon forgotten, until now.
The government's proposed goods and services tax has changed all of that. The requisite honks of protest from our Canadian goose have turned into a terrified squall as it fights being throttled in the process of being plucked.

Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fifth Edition, citation No. 223, paragraph 2, states very clearly:
A Member must be in his own seat should he wish to vote and
